The three opinions regarding the openings (al-fawātiḥ), that is, those I mentioned at the beginning of al-Kashshāf revealing the realities of the Revelation, are those upon which the discerning and skilled scholars rely.

"Mā anzalnā" (We have not sent down): if you take "Ṭāhā" as a counting of the names of the letters in the manner mentioned earlier, then it is the beginning of a statement. If you take it as a name of the sūrah, it may be a predicate referring to it, while it stands in the position of the subject; and "al-Qurʾān" is apparent, placed in the position of the pronoun, because they are Qurʾān; and it may be a response to them, and they are an oath.

It was also read: "mā nazala ʿalayka al-Qurʾāna li-tashqā" (We did not send down the Qurʾān upon you to be wretched), meaning: to tire yourself through excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your anguish that they should believe, like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them﴾. It was said: Abu Jahl and al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith said to him: "You are wretched, for you have abandoned the religion of your fathers." So it was intended to refute that: the religion of Islam and this Qurʾān is the path to attaining every success and the cause of attaining every happiness, while what the disbelievers hold is wretchedness itself.

It is related that he, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed through the night until his feet swelled, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you." However, the first had to come with the lām, because it is not the agent of the verb being caused, so it lost the condition for being put in the accusative as an object. I say: Yes, but that accusative is incidental, like the accusative in ﴿And Moses chose his people﴾. As for the accusative in "tadhkiratan," it is like that in "I struck Zayd," because it is one of the five objects, which are foundations and rules for others.

I say: No, because the two kinds differ, but it is in the accusative as an exception that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), in which "illā" means "but." Its complement cannot be other than: either "tanzīlan" itself, so it falls as its relative clause, or something omitted, so it falls as its qualifier. It is also permissible that "anzalnā" be a quotation of the speech of Gabriel and the angels who descended with him.

Describing the heavens as "the highest" is an indication of the greatness of the power of the One who creates the like of them in their height and the distance of their ascent.

If you read it in the nominative as a laudatory construction, what is its position? I say: if you read it in the genitive, the clause is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject and nothing else. If you read it in the nominative, it may be that, and it may be that it, together with *al-Rahmān*, forms two predicates of the subject.

Since establishing oneself on the Throne, which is the king's couch, accompanies kingship, they used it as a metonymy (*kināya*) for kingship. They say "So-and-so established himself on the throne," meaning he became king, even if he never sat on the couch at all. They also used it because it was famous for that meaning and because it equals "king" in what it conveys, though it is more explicit, more expansive, and more indicative of the picture of the matter.

Similar to this is your saying: "So-and-so's hand is outstretched" and "So-and-so's hand is shackled," meaning he is generous or stingy. There is no difference between the two expressions except what you have mentioned. Indeed, one who never extended his hand in giving, or who had no hand at all, is described as "his hand is outstretched," because for them it is equivalent to saying "he is generous." From this is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ﴾ (The Jews say, "God's hand is shackled") meaning He is stingy, and ﴿بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ﴾ (Rather, His two hands are outstretched) meaning He is generous, without imagining a hand, a shackle, or an outstretching. Interpreting it as "blessing," and forcing the dual form into that meaning, comes from narrowness of mind and from being far removed from the science of eloquence ('ilm al-bayān), which is a journey of years.

That is, He knows what you confide to someone else and what you conceal beyond that, which is what you have brought to mind. Or it means what you keep secret within yourself, and *akhfa* (more hidden) refers to what you will keep secret in yourself. It is reported from some of them that *akhfa* is a verb: [Mahmud said: "It is the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), though some have said that *akhfa* is a past-tense verb (*fi'l madi*)... etc." Ahmad said: It is not hidden that making it a verb, intransitive both in wording and in meaning, is problematic. Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 20, verses 9–10:

He follows this with the story of Musa (peace be upon him), so that the Prophet (ﷺ) may take him as an example in bearing the burdens of prophethood, the duties of the message, and patience in enduring hardships, so that he may attain success and the praiseworthy station with God.

It is permissible for idh (إِذْ, "when") to be in the accusative as an adverbial complement to the narrative, because it is an event. Or it may be governed by an implied verb, meaning: "at the time when he saw a fire, such and such occurred." Or it may be a direct object of a verb mentioned, namely "remember" (اذكر).

Musa had asked Shu'ayb (peace be upon them both) for permission to leave for his mother, and he set out with his family. On the way, a son was born to him on a cold, dark, snowy night. He had lost his way, his flock had scattered, he had no water, and he struck his firestarter (زند) but it failed to produce fire [[The note on "fasalada zanduhu" in al-Sihah: "salad al-zand" means when it makes a sound but does not produce fire. (Ea.)]]. At that moment he saw the fire. It was said that it was a Friday night.

امْكُثُوا (imkuthu): "Stay," that is, remain in your place.

Al-iins (الإيناس): clear seeing that leaves no doubt, and from it comes insan al-ayn (the pupil of the eye), because a thing becomes clear through it. Al-ins (الإنس, humankind) is so named for their visibility, just as al-jinn (الجن) is so named for their concealment. It is also said that it means seeing what one is comforted by. Since he had certainly perceived the fire, it was a settled and certain matter, and so he confirmed it for them with the word "inna" (إِنّ, "indeed") to settle their hearts.

As for bringing a firebrand and finding guidance, these were things he anticipated and hoped for, so he framed them in terms of hope and expectation and said "la'alli" (لَعَلِّي, "perhaps I"), and did not state it definitively by saying "innI atikum" (إنى آتِيكُمْ, "indeed I will come to you"), lest he promise what he could not be sure of fulfilling.

Al-qabas (القبس): fire taken from the tip of a stick, a wick, or something else. From it comes "al-miqbasa" (المقبسة), for the thing from which fire is taken, such as a palm frond or the like.

هُدىً (hudan): that is, people who would guide me on the way, or benefit me with their guidance in matters of religion, according to Mujahid and Qatada. This is because the minds of the righteous are absorbed in religious resolve in all their conditions, and no preoccupation distracts them from it. The meaning is: people possessing guidance. Or, when one finds the guides, one has found guidance.

The sense of elevation in عَلَى (ʿalā, "upon") in عَلَى النَّارِ ("upon the fire") is that the people of the fire occupy the place near it, as Sibawayh said regarding "marartu bi-Zayd" (مررت بزيد): it indicates adjacency to a place near Zayd. Or because those who warm themselves by it and enjoy it, standing and sitting around it, are overlooking it. From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"By my life, many eyes have glimpsed toward the light of a fire on a high ground that cuts through (the darkness).
It flares for two shivering men who warm themselves by it, and there spent the night generosity and the Muhalliq (al-Nadā wa al-Muḥalliq).
Two foster-brothers who share a single breast of a mother, beneath a pitch-black night, never separated."

This is by al-A'sha praising al-Muhalliq (with a kasra on the lam). He was so named because his camel bit him on the face, leaving a mark like a ring (ḥalqa). He was from the people of ʿUkaz, was poor, and had ten daughters whom no one desired because of their poverty. He withdrew with them to some remote desert, and al-A'sha stopped at his place. He slaughtered for him his she-camel, having no other, and treated him generously as a host. Al-A'sha thought highly of him. When he rose in the morning and mounted his riding-beast, he said to him: "Do you have a need?"

He said: "Yes, that you mention my name among the people of ʿUkaz, perhaps someone will desire my daughters, for lean years have afflicted them." So he praised him at ʿUkaz, and before long his daughters were betrothed.

Wa-lahat (ولاحت): meaning he glimpsed and looked out. Al-yafa' (اليفاع): the high ground. Yakhriq (يخرق): that is, the light cuts through and spreads over the land. It is also transmitted as tuhriq (تحرق), with the unmarked ḥāʾ, the pronoun referring to the fire. Tusibbu (تشب) is passive, from "shibbaytu al-nar, ashibbuha shabban wa shubuwwan," meaning I kindled it. The muqarran (المقروران) are those afflicted by cold, that is, by chill; he means by them al-Nadā and al-Muḥalliq, meaning that he and his generosity are constant companions of the fire of hospitality, just as the one who is cold constantly stays by the fire for warmth, and he explained this by saying: "and there spent the night generosity and the Muhalliq."

It is also permissible that al-A'sha meant himself and al-Muhalliq, because the first is more effective in praise. The meaning of their being "upon it" is that they are on its two sides, and because the one warming himself is higher than it, so that he can extend his hand above it. Conjoining al-Muhalliq with al-Nadā indicates that they are inseparable and always together, and he explained this by saying: "two foster-brothers," which is a circumstantial clause describing them, likening them to twins to show the utmost inseparability, even in the womb, and even before it.

Al-laban (اللبان): specifically a woman's milk, and it is in construct with thady umm (ثدي أم, "breast of a mother"), and its tanwin (nunation) is for singularity, and its being annexed to it is because it comes from it. It is also permissible to make it indefinite with tanwin.

Fa-thady (فثدى): is an apposition to it. Al-asḥam (الأسحم): the black, pitch-dark, obscure night; that is, they swore an oath as is also transmitted, in a dark night. Or in the dark womb.

ʿAwḍ (عوض): an adverb of future time, in the accusative governed by what follows it. Lā natafarraq (لا نتفرق): the answer of the oath. All of this is a metaphor for the intensity of the inseparability between him and generosity.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿إِنِّي﴾ with a fatha, meaning: he was called with the words that "I am your Lord" (أَنَا رَبُّكَ). The rest read it with a kasra, meaning: he was called and it was said, "O Musa." Alternatively, because the call (nida', a summons or address) is a kind of speech, it is treated as speech.

The repetition of the pronoun in ﴿إِنِّي أَنَا رَبُّكَ﴾ serves to emphasize the indication, confirm the knowledge, and remove doubt. It is reported that when he was called, "O Musa," he said: "Who is speaking?" Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to him: "Indeed I am your Lord." It is also reported that Iblis whispered to him, saying: "Perhaps you are hearing the speech of a devil." He replied: "I know that it is the speech of Allah, because I hear it from all six of my directions, and I hear it with all my limbs."

It is reported that when he reached [the spot], he saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire blazing [[The wording "as if it were a white fire blazing" differs from al-Khazin's wording, "fire surrounded it," and from al-Nasafi's wording, which replaces "he saw a tree..." with "he found a white fire blazing in a green tree from its top to its bottom, and it was a tree of jujube or boxthorn" (ع).]]. He heard the glorification of the angels and saw a great light, so he feared and was dazed. Then tranquility was cast upon him, and then he was called. The tree was a boxthorn (`awsaja). It is reported: whether he drew near or moved away, what he heard of the voice did not differ.

From Ibn Ishaq: when he drew near, [the tree] withdrew from him. When he saw that, he turned back and felt fear within himself. When he wanted to return, [the tree] came close to him again, and then he was addressed.

It is said that he was commanded to remove his sandals because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey that had not been tanned, according to al-Suddi and Qatada. [[I have not seen it in this form. In al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), it is stated: "On the day Allah spoke to Musa, he wore a woolen cloak and two sandals of the skin of a dead donkey that had not been slaughtered properly."]]

It is said that he was commanded to remove them so that he could touch the valley with his feet, seeking its blessing. It is also said that going barefoot is humility before Allah; for this reason, the early generations (al-salaf) performed the circumambulation of the Ka'ba barefoot, and some of them regarded entering the mosque in sandals as a serious matter, and whenever one of them slipped and entered wearing sandals, he would give charity. The Qur'an indicates that this is respect for the sacred place, exalting it and honoring its sanctity.

It is reported that he removed his sandals and threw them from behind the valley, Tuwa. Tuwa may be read with a damma or a kasra, and it may be treated as diptote (declined partially) or non-diptote (undeclined), interpreted as a place or an area. It is also said: "twice," like thunna (a form meaning "twice," a repetition). [[The phrase "It is said: twice, like thunna" corresponds to al-Jawhari's al-Sihah: some said, regarding Allah's words ﴿بِالْوادِ الْمُقَدَّسِ طُوىً﴾, that tuwa means "twice," i.e., holy. Also in al-Sihah: "al-thunna" (a form), a matter repeated twice, etc. So the original wording was probably also: "It is said: tuwa twice, meaning sanctified and purified twice." The apparent sense of the expression is that tuwa is like thunna in meaning "twice," i.e., Musa was called twice, or the valley was sanctified twice, so it is either an object of nudiya (was called) or of al-muqaddas (the sanctified) (ع).]] That is, he was called two calls, or the valley was sanctified again and again.

﴿وَأَنَا اخْتَرْتُكَ﴾: I have chosen you and selected you for prophethood. Hamza read it as ﴿وإنا اخترناك﴾ ("and We have chosen you").

﴿لِما يُوحى﴾: for what is revealed, i.e., to the one who is being revealed to, or to the revelation. The lam is connected either to "listen" (istama') or to "I have chosen you."

﴿لِذِكْرِي﴾: so that you may remember Me, for My remembrance is that I am worshipped and prayed to. Or: so that you may remember Me in it, because prayer includes remembrances, according to Mujahid. Or: because I have mentioned it in the books and commanded it. Or: so that I may remind you with praise and commendation and make for you a tongue of truth. Or: for a special remembrance that is not mixed with the remembrance of anyone else; or for sincerity in My remembrance and seeking My face, not showing off with it and not intending any other aim. Or: so that you may be one who remembers Me and does not forget, like the deeds of the sincere ones, who keep the remembrance of their Lord in their minds and devote their resolve and thoughts to it, as He said: ﴿لا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجارَةٌ وَلا بَيْعٌ عَنْ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Neither trade nor sale distracts them from the remembrance of Allah"). Or: for the appointed times of My remembrance, which are the times of prayer, as in His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الصَّلاةَ كانَتْ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ كِتاباً مَوْقُوتاً﴾ ("Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times"). The lam here is like it in your saying, "I came to you at such-and-such a time," and that was after six nights had passed. And His saying: ﴿يا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ لِحَياتِي﴾ ("Would that I had sent forth [good deeds] for my life"). It has been interpreted as the remembrance of prayer after forgetting it, from his peace be upon him saying: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it [[Agreed upon (متفق عليه), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra concerning the story of sleeping through the prayer. At its end: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿أَقِمِ الصَّلاةَ لِذِكْرِي﴾ ("Establish prayer for My remembrance"), and in another narration "for dhikrā." This is also agreed upon, from the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet, with the wording: "Whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, its expiation is that he prays it when he remembers it." al-Bukhari added in one narration: "Establish prayer for My remembrance."]]." The proper wording would have been "for its remembrance," as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "when he remembers it." Those who strain to justify it say: when one remembers the prayer, he has remembered Allah. Or by supposing an omitted genitive, meaning: for the remembrance of My prayer. Or because remembrance and forgetting are in reality from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿لِلذِّكْرى﴾ ("for the remembrance").

It is also reported that Iblis whispered to him, saying: "Perhaps you are hearing the speech of a devil." He replied: "I know that it is the speech of Allah, because I hear it from all six of my directions, and I hear it with all my limbs."

It is reported that when he reached [the spot], he saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire blazing [[The wording "as if it were a white fire blazing" differs from al-Khazin's wording, "fire surrounded it," and from al-Nasafi's wording, which replaces "he saw a tree..." with "he found a white fire blazing in a green tree from its top to its bottom, and it was a tree of jujube or boxthorn" (ع).]]. He heard the glorification of the angels and saw a great light, so he feared and was dazed. Then tranquility was cast upon him, and then he was called. The tree was a boxthorn (`awsaja). It is reported: whether he drew near or moved away, what he heard of the voice did not differ.

From Ibn Ishaq: when he drew near, [the tree] withdrew from him. When he saw that, he turned back and felt fear within himself. When he wanted to return, [the tree] came close to him again, and then he was addressed.

It is said that he was commanded to remove his sandals because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey that had not been tanned, according to al-Suddi and Qatada. [[I have not seen it in this form. Its meaning: "I almost conceal it," so that I do not say, "It is coming," because of my intense desire to conceal it. Had it not been for the kindness (lutf) in announcing its coming while keeping its time hidden, I would not have informed you of it. It was also said: the meaning is "I almost conceal it from myself," but there is no indication in the speech of this omitted element, and an omitted element with no indication is discarded. What deluded them about it is that in the codex of Ubayy it reads: "I almost conceal it from myself." And in some codices: "I almost conceal it from myself, so how would I make you aware of it?"

And from Abu al-Darda' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: akhfiha with a fatha on the hamza, from khafah (to conceal), meaning he revealed it, i.e., its manifestation is near, like His saying, ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar 1]. It has also come in some dialects that akhfahu means khafahu (to conceal). By this interpretation is explained the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you bury the disease, we shall not conceal it,
and if you stir up war, we shall not sit back."

It is said: khafahu means he concealed it, and khafahu also means he revealed it, and this is of that type. The meaning: if you conceal the rancors between us, we too conceal them and do not reveal them. He likened the rancor and enmity to a disease, with the common factor being that harm arises from each, by way of explicit metaphor (tasrihiyya).

He likened war to an animal by way of implicit metaphor (makniyya), and "stirring up" (ba'th) is an imaginative depiction (takhyil). Or "stirring up" is used in the sense of causation as a loose metonymy (majaz mursal), or as an explicit metaphor. The meaning: if you display hatred and kindle the fire of battle, we shall defeat you, as you know of us.

﴿Almost I conceal it﴾ admits of both meanings. ﴿That every soul may be recompensed﴾ is connected to ﴿for what it strives﴾, by its striving.

Its meaning: "Let him not turn you away from believing in it." The pronoun refers to the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the prayer (al-salah).

If you say: the expression is a prohibition addressed to the one who does not believe, against his turning Musa away, whereas the intended meaning is a prohibition to Musa against denying the Resurrection (al-ba'th), or a command to him to affirm it. How, then, is this expression suitable for conveying this meaning? I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that the unbeliever's turning one away from believing in it is a cause of denial, so the cause is mentioned in order to indicate the effect. The second is that the unbeliever's turning one away results from the slackness of a man in his religion and the softness of his resolve, so the effect is mentioned in order to indicate the cause, as in their saying: "I shall not see you here," meaning a prohibition against his being seen and being present in his presence, and that is the cause of seeing him. So mentioning the effect serves as evidence of the cause, as if it were said: "Then be firm of resolve and sound of constitution [[His saying "sound of constitution" (ṣalīb al-mu'jam): in al-Sihah, 'ajamtu al-'ud means I bit the stick to learn its hardness from its pliancy. A man who is ṣalīb al-mu'jam is one who is strong in spirit. (ʿ)]], so that it does not appear to those who disbelieve in the Resurrection that you hope to turn you away from what you are upon." The meaning is: those who do not believe in the Hereafter are the vast multitude, for nothing is more agreeable to the disbelievers, and none is more vehemently opposed to them, than the Resurrection. So do not be overawed by the abundance of their rabble nor by the greatness of their numbers, and do not let multitude become a slip for your foot. Know that although they are so numerous, their leader in what they are in is desire and the following of it, not proof and its contemplation. In this is a great exhortation to act upon evidence, a forceful warning against blind imitation (taqlid), and a notice that ruin and destruction lie with imitation and its adherents.

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ Like His saying ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ (11:72), with the accusative of ḥāl (circumstantial accusative; a noun describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) and in the sense of pointing. It is also permissible for ﴿tilka﴾ to be a relative noun (ism mawṣūl; a noun that requires a following clause to complete its meaning), with ﴿bi-yamīnika﴾ as its clause. He asked him only so that He might show him the magnitude of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would bring about in the dry wood, turning it into a live, writhing serpent [[His words "a live, writhing serpent" mean that it moves its tongue in its mouth. This is reported from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]], and so that the great difference between what it was changed from and what it was changed into would be fixed in his mind, and so that he would be alerted to His overwhelming power. An example of this is that an armourer shows you a lump of iron and asks, "What is this?" and you say, "A lump of iron." Then after some days he shows you a finished coat of mail and says, "It is that same lump, which I have made into what you see of marvellous craftsmanship and elegant links." Ibn Abi Ishaq read ʿaṣiyy, in the dialect of Hudhayl.

And similar to it is ﴿yā bushrā﴾ (12:19). They wanted to make the vowel before the first-person ya' kasra, but could not, so they changed the alif into a sister of the kasra. Al-Ḥasan read ʿaṣāyā with a kasra on the ya' because of the meeting of two sukūns, and it is like the reading of Ḥamza, ﴿bi-muṣrikhiyya﴾ (14:22). It is also reported from Ibn Abi Ishaq: sukūn on the ya'.

﴿I lean upon it﴾: I rely on it when I am weary, or when I stop at the head of the flock and during the leap [[His words "the leap" mean the jump. (ʿ)]].

﴿And I beat down with it upon my flock﴾: hashsh al-waraq means to beat it, that is, I beat it down over the heads of my sheep so that they may eat it.

It is related from Luqman ibn ʿAd: "I ate a ḥiqq, a son of a she-camel, and a jadhʿ." And a verse:

"Hashsha Nakhb and Wasīl pushed,
and praise be to Allah, without satiety,"

which I heard from more than one Arab. Nakhb is a valley near al-Ṭā'if, abounding in lote trees.

In the reading of al-Nakhaʿī: ﴿aham﴾ (with hamza), and both derive from hashsh al-khubz, "the bread crumbles," meaning it breaks because of its brittleness. It is related from ʿIkrima: ﴿ahass﴾ with a sīn, meaning I incline over them, scolding them. And al-hass is driving sheep.

He mentioned in detail and in summary the benefits connected with the staff. It is as if He sensed what would follow this question of a great matter that Allah, Exalted, would bring about, so He said: ﴿It is only a staff﴾, which benefits only the benefits of its kind, as canes do, so that His answer would correspond to the purpose He understood from the content of his Lord's speech. It is also permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to enumerate the many uses He had attached to the staff, magnifying and exalting them, and then immediately showed him the great sign, as if He were saying to him: "Where are you from this supreme benefit and greatest need, before which every benefit and need you used to count and take pride in is forgotten?"

They said: He asked him only to make him relax and to lessen his awe. They said: Musa was brief only so that He would ask him about those needs and thereby increase his honour. They said: His tongue was cut off by awe, so he was brief. They said: the name of the staff was nabʿa (a type of wood). It was said regarding ﴿maʾārib﴾ (needs): it had two prongs and a crook. When the branch was long, he bent it with the crook; when he wanted to break it, he twisted it with the two prongs; when he travelled, he placed it on his shoulder and hung his tools from it: the bow, the quiver, the milk-vessel, and others. When he was in the wilderness, he planted it, spread his firesticks [[His words "firesticks" refer to the Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-zand" is the stick by which fire is struck, and it is the upper one; the lower one has a hole in it, and it is the female. When both are brought together they are called zandān, and one does not say zandatān. The plural is zinād, azand and aznād. (Ḥ)]] across its two prongs, cast his cloak over it, and sheltered beneath it. When his rope was short, he joined it to the staff. He used it to fight wild beasts away from his flock.

It was also said that among its miracles was that he drew water with it: it would extend to the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket. At night the two prongs became two candles. When an enemy appeared, it fought on his behalf. When he desired fruit, he planted it and it put forth leaves and bore fruit. He would load his provisions and his water-skin upon it, and it would walk along with him. When he planted it, water would gush forth; when he lifted it, the water would dry up. It also protected him from venomous creatures.

He asked him only so that He might show him the magnitude of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would bring about in the dry wood, turning it into a live, writhing serpent [[His words "a live, writhing serpent" mean that it moves its tongue in its mouth. This is reported from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]], and so that the great difference between what it was changed from and what it was changed into would be fixed in his mind, and so that he would be alerted to His overwhelming power. An example of this is that an armourer shows you a lump of iron and asks, "What is this?" and you say, "A lump of iron." Then after some days he shows you a finished coat of mail and says, "It is that same lump, which I have made into what you see of marvellous craftsmanship and elegant links." Ibn Abi Ishaq read ʿaṣiyy, in the dialect of Hudhayl.

And similar to it is ﴿yā bushrā﴾ (12:19). They wanted to make the vowel before the first-person ya' kasra, but could not, so they changed the alif into a sister of the kasra. Al-Ḥasan read ʿaṣāyā with a kasra on the ya' because of the meeting of two sukūns, and it is like the reading of Ḥamza, ﴿bi-muṣrikhiyya﴾ (14:22). It is also reported from Ibn Abi Ishaq: sukūn on the ya'.

﴿I lean upon it﴾: I rely on it when I am weary, or when I stop at the head of the flock and during the leap [[His words "the leap" mean the jump. (ʿ)]].

﴿And I beat down with it upon my flock﴾: hashsh al-waraq means to beat it, that is, I beat it down over the heads of my sheep so that they may eat it.

It is related from Luqman ibn ʿAd: "I ate a ḥiqq, a son of a she-camel, and a jadhʿ." And a verse:

"Hashsha Nakhb and Wasīl pushed,
and praise be to Allah, without satiety,"

which I heard from more than one Arab. Nakhb is a valley near al-Ṭā'if, abounding in lote trees.

In the reading of al-Nakhaʿī: ﴿aham﴾ (with hamza), and both derive from hashsh al-khubz, "the bread crumbles," meaning it breaks because of its brittleness. It is related from ʿIkrima: ﴿ahass﴾ with a sīn, meaning I incline over them, scolding them. And al-hass is driving sheep.

He mentioned in detail and in summary the benefits connected with the staff. It is as if He sensed what would follow this question of a great matter that Allah, Exalted, would bring about, so He said: ﴿It is only a staff﴾, which benefits only the benefits of its kind, as canes do, so that His answer would correspond to the purpose He understood from the content of his Lord's speech. It is also permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to enumerate the many uses He had attached to the staff, magnifying and exalting them, and then immediately showed him the great sign, as if He were saying to him: "Where are you from this supreme benefit and greatest need, before which every benefit and need you used to count and take pride in is forgotten?"

They said: He asked him only to make him relax and to lessen his awe. They said: Musa was brief only so that He would ask him about those needs and thereby increase his honour. They said: His tongue was cut off by awe, so he was brief. They said: the name of the staff was nabʿa (a type of wood). It was said regarding ﴿maʾārib﴾ (needs): it had two prongs and a crook. When the branch was long, he bent it with the crook; when he wanted to break it, he twisted it with the two prongs; when he travelled, he placed it on his shoulder and hung his tools from it: the bow, the quiver, the milk-vessel, and others. When he was in the wilderness, he planted it, spread his firesticks [[His words "firesticks" refer to the Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-zand" is the stick by which fire is struck, and it is the upper one; the lower one has a hole in it, and it is the female. When both are brought together they are called zandān, and one does not say zandatān. The plural is zinād, azand and aznād. (Ḥ)]] across its two prongs, cast his cloak over it, and sheltered beneath it. When his rope was short, he joined it to the staff. He used it to fight wild beasts away from his flock.

It was also said that among its miracles was that he drew water with it: it would extend to the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket. At night the two prongs became two candles. When an enemy appeared, it fought on his behalf. When he desired fruit, he planted it and it put forth leaves and bore fruit. He would load his provisions and his water-skin upon it, and it would walk along with him. When he planted it, water would gush forth; when he lifted it, the water would dry up. It also protected him from venomous creatures.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 19–20:**

*al-Sa'y* (السعى): walking swiftly, with light and quick movement.

If you ask: why was it mentioned with different words, *al-hayya* (الحية, "the serpent"), *al-jann* (الجان, "the snake/jinn-like serpent"), and *al-tha'ban* (الثعبان, "the great serpent")? I answer: *al-hayya* is a generic noun that applies to the male, the female, the young, and the old. *Al-tha'ban* and *al-jann*, however, are contrasted, because *al-tha'ban* is a large serpent, while *al-jann* is a slender one. There are two explanations for this:

First, at the moment it turned from a staff, it was a serpent, a small yellow slender one, then it swelled and its body grew until it became a *tha'ban*. So *al-jann* refers to its initial state, and *al-tha'ban* to its final state.

Second, it had the form of a *tha'ban*, and the swiftness of its movement was that of a *jann*. The evidence for this is the words of the Most High: ﴿When he saw it writhing as if it were a jann﴾. It was also said that it had a mane like the mane of a horse. It was also said that between its jaws there was forty cubits.

Second, it had the form of a *tha'ban*, and the swiftness of its movement was that of a *jann*. The evidence for this is the words of the Most High: ﴿When he saw it writhing as if it were a jann﴾. It was also said that it had a mane like the mane of a horse. It was also said that between its jaws there was forty cubits.

When he saw that amazing, terrifying event, fear and flight overcame him, as they overcome humans in the face of dreadful and frightening things. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it turned into a huge male serpent that swallowed rocks and trees, so when he saw it swallowing everything he was afraid and fled. It is also reported from some of them: he was only afraid of it because he knew what had happened to Adam through it. It is said: when his Lord said to him, ﴿Do not fear﴾, his fear subsided and his heart was so reassured that he put his hand into its mouth and seized its jaws.

As-sīra (the course, way of conduct) is from the same pattern as ar-rikba (the mount) from ar-rukūb (riding). One says: "So-and-so followed a good course" (sāra fulān sīratan ḥasanatan). Then the word was broadened and came to mean a way or method. It is also said: "the course of the first ones" (sīra al-awwalīn). It is permissible for it to be in the accusative as an adverb of place or time, meaning: We will return it to its first way, that is, in the state it was in when it was a staff. It may also be that ﴿We will restore it﴾ (sanu'īduhā) is a transposed form of ʿāda, meaning "returned to him" (ʿāda ilayhi). From this is the verse of Zuhair:

*"So he cut her rope when she cut it, and the enmity between you and meeting her was a hostile enmity."*

Zuhair's line means: cut off your affection for her, since she cut off her affection for you. He likened affection to a rope by way of explicit metaphor (isti'āra taṣrīḥiyya), and "cutting" (taṣrīm) is a reinforcement (tarshīḥ) and strengthening of the comparison. The word ʿādaka may come from ʿāda, "to return," so the meaning is: it turned you back and sent you away. It may also be a metathesis of ʿadāhu, "to divert him," as nā' is a metathesis of nā'a, so the meaning is: it diverted you. Abū ʿUmayr said: ʿādaka means "occupied you." Al-Aṣma'ī said it means both "returned to you" and "diverted you."

It is well known that when a verb is intransitive, it becomes transitive to its object by means of the hamza by analogy (qiyās), and when it is transitive to one object by itself, it becomes transitive to two objects by adding the hamza to it. It has been disputed whether this is analogical or transmitted (samā'ī).

Its use with ʿāda, "to return him," follows the same rule as mentioned. As for its being transitive to "that you meet her" as well, it is by dropping the preposition for broadening (tawassu'). Al-ʿadā' means occupation or distance, and it is also used for injustice, from ʿadā ʿalayhi (he transgressed against him). Al-Jawharī said: al-ʿadā' (with a fatḥa) means injustice, and it may be read with a kasra, meaning "that which prevents," because al-ʿadā' is that by which one is diverted, as al-liwādh is that by which one seeks refuge and ar-ribāṭ is that by which one is tied. The meaning is: cut off her affection, since she cut off your affection. Your being diverted from meeting her is a great diverter, and attributing the diversion to it is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī) of the type of attribution to the cause or the instrument.

It is also possible that the original was ʿadā, with a kasra and short vowel, the plural of ʿadūw (enemy). It was then lengthened for poetic necessity, meaning: enemies prevented you from meeting her, so the attribution is literal (ḥaqīqī).

A third good interpretation is that ﴿We will restore it﴾ is self-standing and not connected to its course. The meaning is that it was created first as a staff, then it went away and was reversed into a serpent. So We will restore it after it has gone, as We created it at first. The accusative of "its course" (sīratahā) is by a hidden verb, meaning: it will proceed in its first course. That is: We will restore it proceeding in its first course, where you used to lean upon it and had in it the uses that you knew.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 22–23:

It is said that each of two sides is a "janah" (wing): like the two wings of an army, for its two flanks (mujannibatayhi). The two sides of a person (janahan al-insan) are his two flanks (janbayhi), and the original metaphorical source is the two wings of a bird. They were called two wings because one folds them (yajnahuhuma) when flying. The meaning is "to your side, beneath the upper arm," and this is shown by His words ﴿تَخْرُجْ﴾ ("it will come forth").

Al-su' (السوء, "harm/evil"): badness and ugliness in anything. By it he refers euphemistically to leprosy (al-baras), just as the private parts are referred to euphemistically as al-saw'ah (السوأة, "the shameful place"). Jadhima, the lord of al-Zabba' [[His words "and Jadhima, the lord of al-Zabba'": Jadhima was the king of al-Hira and al-Zabba' was the queen of al-Jazira, as stated in al-Sihah. (E.)]] was leprous, so they referred to it by "al-abrash" (the spotted one) [[His words "so they referred to it by al-abrash": in al-Sihah, al-barash in a horse means small spots differing from the rest of its colour, and a horse is abrash. (E.)]]. Leprosy is the thing most hateful to the Arabs; they have a great aversion to it, and their ears recoil at its name. So it was fitting that it be referred to euphemistically. We do not see anything more excellent, more refined, or more effective at cutting to the joints than the euphemisms and courtesies of the Qur'an.

It is reported that he was of wheat-brown complexion; he took his hand out from his garment, and it was white, with a radiance like the radiance of the sun, dazzling the sight.

"Bayda'" (white) and "ayah" (sign) are two circumstantial clauses (hal) together. "Min ghayri su'" (without harm) is a complement attached to "bayda'," as you would say "it became white without blemish." There is another possibility for the accusative of "ayah": it is governed by an elided verb such as "take" or "here is," and similar words, the verb being omitted because the context indicates it. The phrase ﴿لِنُرِيَكَ﴾ ("that We may show you") is connected to this elided verb: that is, "take this sign too, after the staff has turned into a serpent, so that We may show you with these two signs some of Our greatest signs." Or: "so that We may show you, with them, the greatest of Our signs."

Or: "so that We may show you of Our greatest signs, We did that."

When he commanded him to go to Pharaoh, the tyrant, may God curse him, Moses understood that he had been charged with a great task and a weighty matter, one that required bearing what only a steady-hearted man with a broad breast could bear. So he asked his Lord to expand his breast and widen his heart, and to make him forbearing and able to endure, so that he could face whatever hardships might come upon him, hardships that would cause the patience of the patient to fail, with gracious endurance and firm steadfastness. He also asked that his task, which is the caliphate of God on earth, along with what accompanies it of undertaking great affairs and bearing grave calamities, be made easy for him in general.

If you ask: what is the benefit of the word "for me" (لِي) in His words ﴿Lord, expand for me my breast and ease for me my task﴾, and is the statement not complete without it? I say:

[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask what is the benefit of 'for me' when the sentence is complete without it..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: "It is possible in my view, and God knows best, that its benefit is the acknowledgment that the benefit of expanding the breast returns to him and accrues to him. God, Mighty and Majestic, does not benefit from sending him, nor does He seek help from expanding his breast, exalted and sanctified be He, unlike the messenger of a king, when he is asked to do something for him, for what is asked of him is something whose benefit returns to the one who sent him, and his purpose in his mission is attained. And God knows best."]

The statement is complete without it. [I say:] The speech was first made vague, so it was said: "Expand for me and ease for me," and thus it was understood that there is something expanded and something eased. Then it was clarified and the vagueness was removed by mentioning them, so it was more emphatic in asking for the expansion and ease of his breast and his task than saying: "Expand my breast and ease my task" in plain clarity, because the former repeats one meaning in the two ways of generality and specification.

On the authority of Ibn Abbas: there was an impediment (رتة) in his tongue, because of what was narrated in the hadith of the ember (حديث الجمرة). [Al-Zamakhshari's note: "The Sihah says that 'ratah' with a dammah means a foreignness in speech. The hadith of the ember: Musa was playing before Pharaoh with a staff in his hand, and he struck Pharaoh's head with it. Pharaoh became angry and intended to kill him, but his wife said to him: 'He is a child who does not understand; test him if you wish.' So she brought two basins, one with embers and the other with jewels. Musa reached his hand toward the jewels, but Gabriel turned it toward the embers, and he put an ember in his mouth and his tongue was burned."]

[Al-Zamakhshari's note: "I have not seen it in this form. It occurs in the long hadith of the qunut which al-Nasa'i and others narrated through al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: 'I asked Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, about the words of God Most High, ﴿and We tested you with a testing﴾,' and he mentioned it at length over four pages, including the story of Asiya and Pharaoh. In it she says: 'Bring near to him two embers and two pearls,' and he took the two embers, but she snatched them from him, fearing they would burn his hand. This indicates that he did not raise them to his mouth, and this is the most authentic of what has been transmitted about it. Al-Hakim narrated through Wahb ibn Munabbih a story in which she says: 'Test him. If you wish, put in this a coal and gold, and see which one he grasps.' He said: 'He took the ember and placed it in his mouth, then threw it out when he found its heat.' It is said that the knot which was in Musa's tongue was from the effect of that ember which he put in his mouth."]

It is also narrated that his hand was burned, and that Pharaoh strove to treat it but it did not heal. When Musa called him, Pharaoh said: "To which Lord are you calling me?" He said: "To the One who heals my hand, though you were unable to heal it."

It is also reported from some scholars that his hand did not heal so that it would not enter into one bowl with Pharaoh, for then a bond of eating together would be established between them.

Scholars differed about whether the impediment was completely removed. It was said: some of it went away and some of it remained, based on the words of God Most High, ﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent than I in speech﴾, and His words, ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾. [Al-Zamakhshari's note: "In the tongue of al-Husayn ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, there was an impediment." I have not found this. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "He inherited it from his uncle Musa."] It was also said: it was completely removed, based on the words of God Most High, ﴿You have been given your request, O Musa﴾.

Regarding the indefiniteness of "a knot" (عقدة), though he did not say "a knot in my tongue": he asked for the untying of part of it, wishing to be understood well, and he did not seek complete eloquence. The phrase ﴿from my tongue﴾ (مِنْ لِسَانِي) is a qualifier of "knot," as if it were said: "a knot from the knots of my tongue."

The word "wazir" (وزير) is from the root "wizr" (وزر), because he bears the burden on behalf of the king, or because of his burdens and responsibilities. Or it is from "wizr" [Al-Zamakhshari's note: "'Wizr' means a heavy load. 'Or from wizr' means a refuge, as the Sihah states."], because the king relies on his opinion and turns to him in his affairs. Or it is from "mu'azarah" (مؤازرة), which means assistance. On the authority of al-Asma'i he said: "The analogical form would have been 'azir,' but the hamza was changed to a waw. The reason for changing it is that the pattern fa'il came to mean mufa'il in a suitable way, as in their saying: 'ashir' (companion), 'jalis' (companion), 'qa'id' (sitting companion), 'khalil' (close friend), 'sadiq' (friend), and 'nadim' (boon companion). So when it was changed in 'akhih' (his brother), it was changed in it too. Assigning a thing to its counterpart is not rare, and it was also done with a view to yuwazir (يوازر) and its derivatives, and to the mu'azarah."

[Regarding the grammar of ﴿wazīran﴾ and ﴿Harun﴾:] ﴿wazīran﴾ and ﴿Hārūn﴾ are the objects of the verb ﴿make﴾ (اجْعَلْ). The second is placed before the first to give attention to the matter of the wazirate. Or, the two objects are ﴿for me, a wazir﴾, and ﴿Harun﴾ is an explicative appositive (عطف بيان) of "wazir." ﴿My brother﴾ (أَخِي) in both cases is a substitute (بدل) of ﴿Harun﴾. If it is made a second explicative appositive, it is permissible and good.

All read ﴿Strengthen﴾ (اشْدُدْ) and ﴿make him share﴾ (وَأَشْرِكْهُ) as supplications. Ibn Amir alone read: ﴿I strengthen﴾ (اشدد) and ﴿I make him share﴾ (أشركه), as answers [i.e., as first-person resultative forms].

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "my brother and strengthen." From Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "make him a partner in my affair, and strengthen my back through him."

For one who reads in the imperative form, it is permissible to make ﴿my brother﴾ (أَخِي) nominative as the subject (مبتدأ), with ﴿strengthen with him﴾ (وَاشْدُدْ بِهِ) as its predicate, and to stop at ﴿Harun﴾.

"Azr" (الأزر) means strength, and "azarahu" (أزره) means he strengthened him. That is: make him my partner in the message, so that we may cooperate in worshipping You and remembering You, for cooperation, because it stirs desires, increases and multiplies good. ﴿Indeed You are ever Seeing of us﴾ (إِنَّكَ كُنْتَ بِنا بَصِيراً), that is, knowing our circumstances and that mutual support is something that benefits us, and that Harun is an excellent helper and supporter of my arm, since he is older than me in years and more eloquent in speech.

The word "wazir" (وزير) is from the root "wizr" (وزر), because he bears the burden on behalf of the king, or because of his burdens and responsibilities. Or it is from "wizr" [Al-Zamakhshari's note: "'Wizr' means a heavy load. 'Or from wizr' means a refuge, as the Sihah states."], because the king relies on his opinion and turns to him in his affairs. Or it is from "mu'azarah" (مؤازرة), which means assistance. On the authority of al-Asma'i he said: "The analogical form would have been 'azir,' but the hamza was changed to a waw. The reason for changing it is that the pattern fa'il came to mean mufa'il in a suitable way, as in their saying: 'ashir' (companion), 'jalis' (companion), 'qa'id' (sitting companion), 'khalil' (close friend), 'sadiq' (friend), and 'nadim' (boon companion). So when it was changed in 'akhih' (his brother), it was changed in it too. Assigning a thing to its counterpart is not rare, and it was also done with a view to yuwazir (يوازر) and its derivatives, and to the mu'azarah."

[Regarding the grammar of ﴿wazīran﴾ and ﴿Harun﴾:] ﴿wazīran﴾ and ﴿Hārūn﴾ are the objects of the verb ﴿make﴾ (اجْعَلْ). The second is placed before the first to give attention to the matter of the wazirate. Or, the two objects are ﴿for me, a wazir﴾, and ﴿Harun﴾ is an explicative appositive (عطف بيان) of "wazir." ﴿My brother﴾ (أَخِي) in both cases is a substitute (بدل) of ﴿Harun﴾. If it is made a second explicative appositive, it is permissible and good.

All read ﴿Strengthen﴾ (اشْدُدْ) and ﴿make him share﴾ (وَأَشْرِكْهُ) as supplications. Ibn Amir alone read: ﴿I strengthen﴾ (اشدد) and ﴿I make him share﴾ (أشركه), as answers [i.e., as first-person resultative forms].

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "my brother and strengthen." From Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "make him a partner in my affair, and strengthen my back through him."

For one who reads in the imperative form, it is permissible to make ﴿my brother﴾ (أَخِي) nominative as the subject (مبتدأ), with ﴿strengthen with him﴾ (وَاشْدُدْ بِهِ) as its predicate, and to stop at ﴿Harun﴾.

"Azr" (الأزر) means strength, and "azarahu" (أزره) means he strengthened him. That is: make him my partner in the message, so that we may cooperate in worshipping You and remembering You, for cooperation, because it stirs desires, increases and multiplies good. ﴿Indeed You are ever Seeing of us﴾ (إِنَّكَ كُنْتَ بِنا بَصِيراً), that is, knowing our circumstances and that mutual support is something that benefits us, and that Harun is an excellent helper and supporter of my arm, since he is older than me in years and more eloquent in speech.

Al-Su'l: the request or petition. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like your saying "khubz" meaning "makhbuz" (baked bread), and "akl" meaning "ma'kul" (that which is eaten).

The revelation to the mother of Moses may take one of several forms. It may be through the tongue of a prophet in her time, as in His saying ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ (5:111). Or He may send to her an angel, not in the manner of prophethood, as He sent to Mary. Or He may show her this in a dream, so that she becomes aware of it. Or He may inspire her, as in His saying ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾ (16:68). That is, We revealed to her a matter for which there is no way to attain it or to know it except through revelation, and in which there is a religious benefit, so it had to be revealed and not left out. In other words, it is something that must necessarily be revealed, and it is a great matter, and something like it deserves to be revealed. The *'an* (that) here is *mufassira* (explanatory), because *wahy* (revelation) carries the sense of speech.

The verb *qadhf* (casting) is used in the sense of throwing and placing. From it comes His saying ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ (33:26). Likewise *ramy* (throwing) is used. A poet said:

A youth whom God pelted with beauty while he was in his prime,
who saw me, when my condition was what it was, Umaylah complained
to one whose wealth was his own: he supported me and did not desert me.

When he saw that glory had been borrowed as garments,
he wore a robe with a long, flowing hem and girded himself.

A youth whom God pelted with beauty while in his prime,
he has a mark that is not hard on the eye.

As if the Pleiades were hung upon his chest,
and on his nose is the Sirius, and on his cheek the moon.

These verses are by Usayd ibn 'Unqa' al-Fazari. He was one of the greatest people of his time and the most learned in literature. His life was prolonged and his age afflicted him. Umaylah al-Fazari met him, greeted him, and said: "What has brought you, uncle, to what I see?" He said: "One like you withholds his wealth, and I preserve my face from asking people."

Umaylah said: "If you remain until tomorrow, I will change your condition." When it was the time of dawn, he heard the braying of camels and the neighing of horses under the wealth. He said: "What is this?" They said: "Umaylah has given half his wealth to you and to himself." So he composed this poem.

He likened his wealth to a barren she-camel, by way of *makniyya* (metonymy). The complaint to it is an imaginative representation (*takhyil*). The pronoun in *wasa* means "he gave" to Umaylah. It is also permissible that it refers to the wealth, based on the earlier comparison. The "garments of glory" are a figure for noble deeds and generosity by way of *tasrih* (explicit metaphor), and borrowing them is an *tarshih* (supporting elaboration). The meaning is that he took them from their owners and they departed from their companions. All of this is a metonymy for the generosity of the wealthy. *Sabigh al-dhayl* means one with a long hem. *Iqtazara* means he put on a waistcloth. It is read with the *ta'* doubled. It is also permissible to read it with the *ta'* vowelled and a sukun *hamza* before it, on the original form and the figurative usage as stated above. This is a metonymy for the abundance of his generosity. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when he saw that people boast only of the glories of others, he himself performed noble deeds for himself. *Ramahu Allah bi-l-husn* means He placed beauty in him abundantly, as if He cast it into him without measure. *Yafi'* means a young man in his prime, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. *Al-simiyya'* is the mark that is not hard on the eye, a metonymy for its clarity, so that it needs no reflection, like the appearance of stars. *Al-nahr* is the upper part of the chest and the lower part of the neck. *Al-Shi'ra'* is a star of great brightness. The second verse explains the first. It is also transmitted as "*hiba' Allah*" (the gift of God), and as "*'allaqat fi jabinihi*" (hung upon his forehead), and as "*wa fi jidihi al-qamar*" (and on his neck the moon). *Hiba'* means he gave. *Al-jid* means the neck. This last transmission is more firmly established.

That is, beauty came to be in him and was placed in him. All the pronouns refer to Moses. If some of them refer to him and some to the chest, that is a defect, because it leads to the discord of the composition (*nazm*). If you say: the one cast into the sea is the chest, and likewise the one thrown onto the shore. I reply: what harm would it do you to say: the one cast and the one thrown is Moses within the chest, so that the pronouns do not divide and the composition does not become discordant for you? Since it was God's will and purpose that the flowing of the sea's current should not fail to bring him to the shore, and that it should cast him there, a figurative path was taken, and the sea was treated as if it had discernment. It was commanded to do so, so that it would obey the command and comply with its order. Thus it was said ﴿Let the sea cast him onto the shore﴾ (20:39).

It is related that they placed in the chest cotton that had been carded, then they put him in it, plastered it, and sealed it with pitch, then cast it into the sea. A great river ran from the sea to the garden of Pharaoh. While he was sitting at the edge of a pool with Asiya, behold, there was the chest. He ordered it brought out and opened, and there was a child whose face was the most beautiful of all people. The enemy of God loved him intensely, so much that he could not endure being apart from him.

The apparent meaning of the wording is that the sea cast him on its shore, which is its bank, because the water scrapes (*yahsaluhu*), that is, peels off, and cast him there, and he was picked up from the shore. Unless the sea cast him at a place on the shore where there was the mouth of Pharaoh's river, and then the river carried him to the pool.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ (20:39). The phrase *minni* (from Me) either relates to *ulqaytu* (I cast), so the meaning is: I loved you, and whom God loves, hearts love. Or it relates to a deleted element which is a description of *mahabba* (love), meaning: a love that is established or occurs from Me, which I have fixed and planted in hearts. For this reason Pharaoh and everyone who saw you loved you.

It is related that there was on his face a trace of beauty, and in his eyes a charm, so that no one who saw him could turn away from him. ﴿And that you might be reared under My eye﴾ (20:39): that you might be brought up and treated kindly, and I would be watching over you and observing you, just as a man watches a thing with his eyes when he cares for it. You say to a craftsman: "Make this under my eye," meaning, "I watch you, so that you do not deviate from my intention and my desire."

*Wa li-tusna'a* is conjoined to a hidden cause, like: "that he may show compassion to you and be fond of you" (*li-yata'attafa 'alayka wa tura'imma*), and similar. Or its explained cause is deleted, meaning: "and that you be made, I did that." It is read as *wa li-tusna'a* and *wa li-tusna'a*, with the *lam* vowelled with a kasra and with a sukun. The jussive is because it is a command.

It is also read as *wa li-tusna'a* with the *ta'* vowelled with a fatha and in the accusative, meaning: "and that your work and your conduct may be under My eye."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 40–41:

The governing element (al-'amil) in ﴿when you were walking﴾ is "I cast" or "that you may be raised (watched over)." It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿when We revealed﴾.

If you say: how can a substitution be valid when the two times are different and far apart? I answer: just as it is valid, even though the time is extended and its two ends are distant, for a man to say to you: "I met so-and-so in such-and-such a year," and you reply: "I met him at that time too." Indeed, he may have met him at the beginning of that period while you met him at its end. It is reported that his sister, whose name was Maryam, came seeking news of him, and she came upon them searching for a wet-nurse for him whose breast he would accept, for he would not accept the breast of any woman. So she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will take care of him?﴾ and she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast.

It is reported that Asiya asked Pharaoh to grant him to her, and she adopted him, and she was the one who showed compassion to him and sought wet-nurses for him.

[Moses] is the same man of the Copts whom the Israelite had called upon him for help against. He killed him when he was twelve years old. He was distressed on account of the killing, fearing the punishment of God and the retaliation of Pharaoh, so God forgave him through his seeking forgiveness when he said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and He saved him from Pharaoh, who would have sunk his claws into him, when he migrated with him to Madyan. ﴿Futunan﴾ may be a verbal noun (masdar) of the pattern fu'ul from a transitive verb, like thubur, shukur and kufur.

The plural of fitn or fitna (with the feminine ta' disregarded, as in hujuz and budur, for hujza and badra) means: We delivered you into various trials. Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "We rescued you from one ordeal after another: you were born in a year when the young boys were being killed; this is one trial, O Ibn Jubayr. Your mother cast you into the river. Pharaoh resolved to kill you. You killed a Copt. You hired yourself out for ten years. You lost the way and your sheep scattered on a dark night." He would say at each one: "This is a trial, O Ibn Jubayr." Fitna means ordeal, and everything that is hard for a human being; and everything with which Allah tests His servants is a fitna. He said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾.

Madyan is eight stages from Egypt. It is reported from Wahb that he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years, of which [the period included] the bride-price for his daughter, and he fulfilled the lesser or the greater of the two terms. That is: it had been decreed in My judgment and My destiny that I speak to you and make you a prophet, at a particular time which I had appointed for that, so you came only in accordance with that measure, neither ahead nor behind. It was said: [it refers to] a measure of time in which revelation is sent to the prophets, namely at the age of forty.

This is an image for the rank of closeness, honour and speech with which He invested him. His state is likened to that of one whom a king selects for the combination of qualities and distinctive features in him, deeming him worthy that no one should be nearer to him in rank or more refined in station, so he favours him with honour and preference, and singles him out for himself.

[Moses] does not see or hear except with His eye and ear, and entrusts the secret of his hidden purpose to none but the very core of his conscience.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 40–41:

The governing element (al-'amil) in ﴿when you were walking﴾ is "I cast" or "that you may be raised (watched over)." It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿when We revealed﴾.

If you say: how can a substitution be valid when the two times are different and far apart? I answer: just as it is valid, even though the time is extended and its two ends are distant, for a man to say to you: "I met so-and-so in such-and-such a year," and you reply: "I met him at that time too." Indeed, he may have met him at the beginning of that period while you met him at its end. It is reported that his sister, whose name was Maryam, came seeking news of him, and she came upon them searching for a wet-nurse for him whose breast he would accept, for he would not accept the breast of any woman. So she said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will take care of him?﴾ and she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast.

It is reported that Asiya asked Pharaoh to grant him to her, and she adopted him, and she was the one who showed compassion to him and sought wet-nurses for him.

[Moses] is the same man of the Copts whom the Israelite had called upon him for help against. He killed him when he was twelve years old. He was distressed on account of the killing, fearing the punishment of God and the retaliation of Pharaoh, so God forgave him through his seeking forgiveness when he said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, and He saved him from Pharaoh, who would have sunk his claws into him, when he migrated with him to Madyan. ﴿Futunan﴾ may be a verbal noun (masdar) of the pattern fu'ul from a transitive verb, like thubur, shukur and kufur.

The plural of fitn or fitna (with the feminine ta' disregarded, as in hujuz and budur, for hujza and badra) means: We delivered you into various trials. Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "We rescued you from one ordeal after another: you were born in a year when the young boys were being killed; this is one trial, O Ibn Jubayr. Your mother cast you into the river. Pharaoh resolved to kill you. You killed a Copt. You hired yourself out for ten years. You lost the way and your sheep scattered on a dark night." He would say at each one: "This is a trial, O Ibn Jubayr." Fitna means ordeal, and everything that is hard for a human being; and everything with which Allah tests His servants is a fitna. He said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾.

It is reported from Wahb that he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years, of which [the period included] the bride-price for his daughter, and he fulfilled the lesser or the greater of the two terms. That is: it had been decreed in My judgment and My destiny that I speak to you and make you a prophet, at a particular time which I had appointed for that, so you came only in accordance with that measure, neither ahead nor behind. It was said: [it refers to] a measure of time in which revelation is sent to the prophets, namely at the age of forty.

This is an image for the rank of closeness, honour and speech with which He invested him. His state is likened to that of one whom a king selects for the combination of qualities and distinctive features in him, deeming him worthy that no one should be nearer to him in rank or more refined in station, so he favours him with honour and preference, and singles him out for himself.

[Moses] does not see or hear except with His eye and ear, and entrusts the secret of his hidden purpose to none but the very core of his conscience.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 42–44:

Al-wany (al-wanā): slackness and falling short. It is also read tanyā, with the vowel of the imperfect prefix pronounced as a kasra for assimilation (ittibāʿ), meaning: do not become slack in remembering Me, and do not cease to be mindful of Me wherever you turn, and take My remembrance as a wing by which you rise, seeking aid and support from Me through it, believing that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through remembering Me. It is also permissible that by "remembrance" is meant the conveying of the message, since remembrance (dhikr) applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is for its sake and the greatest of them, so it deserved to be called by the name of remembrance. It is narrated that God, exalted is He, revealed to Harun while he was in Egypt that he should go out to meet Musa. It was also said that he heard of his coming. And it was said that it was inspired to him. It is read layyinan with a light pronunciation, meaning gentle speech, like the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?﴾ (Qur'an 79:18–19), because its outward form is interrogative and consultative, and presents what it contains of great success. It was also said: He promised him youth that would not age after it, and a kingdom that would not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink and marriage would remain for him until his death. It was also said: do not confront him with what he dislikes, and be gentle with him in speech, because of his right of having raised Musa, and because of what he has of a right similar to that of fatherhood. It was also said:

They addressed him by a kunya, and he is among those who have three kunyas: Abu al-Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah. The "hope" (taraji) belongs to them both, meaning: go with your hope and your desire, and undertake the matter with the diligence of one who hopes and aspires that his work will bear fruit and his effort will not be in vain, so he strives with his utmost capacity and exerts himself to his fullest ability. The benefit of sending them to him, while knowing that he will not believe, is to establish the proof and cut off the excuse: ﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs?﴾ (Qur'an 20:134). That is: ﴿he may take heed or fear﴾ (Qur'an 20:44), that is, he may remember and reflect, and so exert fairness from himself and submit to the truth, or fear that the matter is as you describe, so that his denial drags him into destruction.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 45:

*Farrata* (to precede, to go ahead). From it comes *al-fārit* (the one who goes ahead of the watering party to the water). A *faras farṭ* is a horse that outpaces the other horses, meaning: we fear that he will hasten to punish us and act against us with it. It is also read *yafruṭa*, from *afraṭahu* (he caused him to be hasty), when another makes him take the path of haste. They both feared that someone might prompt him to hasten the punishment [[Maḥmūd said: "The meaning of *yafruṭu ʿalaynā* is that he hastens his punishment of us ... etc." Aḥmad said: Since the etiquette observed here is to leave this expression without its object, it is not far-fetched that the same etiquette calls for acknowledging the favour of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, through the addition of the object in His words *ishrah lī ṣadrī* ("expand for me my breast"), as I mentioned earlier. And Allah knows best.]] from a devil, or from his tyranny, arrogance and claim to divinity, or from his love of leadership, or from his people, the Copts, the rebellious ones about whom the Lord of Might said: ﴿Said the chiefs of his people﴾.

It is also read *yafruṭa*, from *al-ifrāṭ fī al-adhā* (excess in harm), meaning: we fear that he will prevent us from conveying the message by hastening against us, or that he will exceed the limit in punishing us if he does not hasten, based on what we have known and tested of his wickedness and insolence. ﴿Or that he will transgress﴾, by overstepping to the point that he says about you what is not fitting, because of his boldness toward you and the hardness of his heart. In mentioning it in this way, unrestricted and in the manner of allusion, there is a form of good etiquette and avoidance of uttering something grave.

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, on Surah 20, verses 46–48:

﴿Indeed I am with you both﴾, meaning: I am your protector and helper. ﴿I hear and I see﴾, meaning: I hear and see what passes between you and him, of speech and action, and so I will do what my protection and support for you require. It is possible that your words and deeds are decreed, and it is possible that nothing is decreed. It is as if it were said: I am your protector and helper, hearing and seeing. When the protector and helper is like this, protection is complete, support is sound, and concern about the enemy is gone.

The Children of Israel were under the rule of Pharaoh and the Copts, who tormented them by assigning them hard labour: digging, building, carrying stones, and forced labour in everything, along with the killing of the sons and the use of the women. ﴿We have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ is a sentence that follows from the first sentence, ﴿We are indeed two messengers of your Lord﴾, and serves as its clarification and explanation, because a claim to prophethood is not established except by its evidence, which is the bringing of a sign. The phrase ﴿a sign﴾ is stated in the singular and not the dual, though two signs were given, because what is intended in this place is the confirmation of the claim by its proof. It is as if he said: We have come to you with a miracle, a proof and an argument for what we claim of messengership. Likewise ﴿I have indeed come to you with a clear proof from your Lord﴾ (7:73), and ﴿So bring a sign, if you are of the truthful﴾ (7:106), and ﴿Even if I bring you something manifest?﴾ (26:30). He means: peace from the angels, who are the keepers of Paradise, upon the guided, and rebuke from the keepers of the Fire and the punishment upon the deniers.

He addressed the two of them, but directed the call to one of them, Musa (Moses), because he is the principal of prophethood, while Harun (Aaron) was his minister and follower. It is possible that his wickedness and profligacy [[His saying "his wickedness and profligacy" means his corruption and depravity. (ʿ)]] led him to demand that Musa speak rather than his brother, because of what was known of Harun's eloquence and the speech impediment in Musa's tongue. This is indicated by his saying: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾

*Khalqahu* (خَلْقَهُ) is the first object of *aʿṭā* (gave). That is: He gave His creation everything they need and from which they derive benefit. Or it is the second object, meaning: He gave everything its form and shape that corresponds to the benefit assigned to it, just as He gave the eye the shape that suits seeing, the ear the form that suits hearing, and likewise the nose, the hand, the foot and the tongue: each of them corresponds to the benefit attached to it, and none of them substitutes for another. Or it means He gave every animal its counterpart in creation and form, since He made the stallion and the mare [[His saying "and the mare" is pronounced with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and sukūn on the jīm: the female of horses. End of the corrector's note.]] a pair, the camel and the she-camel, and the man and the woman, so that He did not pair anything with a kind other than its own or with what is contrary to its nature.

It is also read *khalqahu* as a qualifier either of the first noun or of the second, meaning: everything God created He did not leave without His gift and bounty. ﴿Then He guided﴾, that is, He made it known how to benefit from what He had given, and how to reach it.

How excellent this answer is, how concise and comprehensive, and how clear it is to one who applies his mind and looks with an eye of fairness and seeks the truth.

Question: he asked about the condition of the generations that passed and departed, and about the wretchedness of those among them who were wretched and the happiness of those who were happy. He answered that this is a question about the unseen (al-ghayb), which God has reserved to Himself, and none knows it but He. "I am only a servant like you; I know of it only what the Knower of the unseen has informed me. The knowledge of the states of the generations is written with God in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz); it is not permissible for God to err in anything or to forget it." It is said: "I went astray from a thing" (dallaltu al-shay') when you missed its place and did not find it, as in your saying "I went astray from the road and the dwelling (al-manzil)." It has also been read as yadilla, from adallahu, meaning he lost it (or caused it to be lost). Ibn 'Abbas said: "He does not leave whoever disbelieved in Him until He takes vengeance upon him, and He does not leave whoever affirmed His oneness until He rewards him."

It is also possible that Pharaoh disputed with him concerning God's encompassing knowledge of everything and His clear accounting of every knowable thing; so he was obstinate and said, "What do you say about the bygone generations, and their numerousness that has extended and the extremities of their numbers that have spread apart? How did He encompass them along with their parts and essences?"

He answered that every existent is encompassed by His knowledge, and it is recorded with Him in a Book, and error and forgetfulness are not permissible for Him, just as they are permissible for you, O humble servant and feeble human. That is: He does not err as you err, nor forget as you forget, O you who claim lordship through ignorance and impudence.

"Who made for you the earth a cradle (mahdan)": the word alladhi is an attribute of my Lord, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by way of praise. This is from its sources and its figurative usage. Mahdan is the reading of the people of Kufa, meaning: He made it a cradle, a cradle-like bed.

Or: they make it smooth (yatamahhadunaha), so it is for them like a cradle (mahd), which is what is prepared for a child.

"And threaded (wa-salaka) for you therein paths": from the words of the Exalted, "What has caused you to enter Saqar?" (74:42); "We cause it to enter (naslukuhu) into the hearts of the criminals" (26:200); that is, He made for you roads in it, and channels through the mountains, valleys and deserts.

"Then We brought forth (fa-akhrajna)": he shifts in it from the third-person form to the first-person plural of the one obeyed, because of what I mentioned of variation (al-iftinan), and to signal that He is obeyed, so that diverse things submit to His command and disparate kinds yield to His will, and nothing can resist His desire. Similar is the words of the Exalted: "It is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing" (6:99); "Do you not see that God sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby fruits of varied colors" (35:27); "Or who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delightful beauty" (27:60). Within it there is also a specification that We are the ones who are able to do the like of this, and no one's power can reach it.

"Kinds (azwajan)": varieties, so called because they are paired and joined with one another. "Diverse (shatta)": an attribute of the kinds, plural of shatit, like marid and marda. It may also be an attribute of the vegetation, as nabat is a verbal noun used for the growing thing, as nabt is, so the singular and plural are alike in it; meaning they are diverse in benefit, taste, color, smell and form, some suited to people and some to animals.

They said: among the blessings of the Mighty and Exalted is that the sustenance of servants is attained through the labor of livestock, and God has made their fodder from what exceeds their needs and what they cannot eat. "Eat and pasture (kulu wa-arga)": a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in fa-akhrajna. The meaning: We brought forth kinds of vegetation, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and to feed some to your livestock.
