The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 55:

He meant by creating them from the earth the creation of their origin, Adam, peace be upon him, from it. It is also said that the angel goes and takes some soil from the place where he is to be buried, and scatters it over the sperm-drop, so that he is created from both the dust and the sperm-drop together. By bringing them out from it, He meant that He reassembles their scattered parts, mixed with the dust, returns them as they were when alive, and brings them out to the place of gathering: ﴿On the Day they will emerge from the graves swiftly﴾. God enumerated the benefits that they derive from the earth, in that He made it for them a bed and a cradle on which they turn, and made in it pathways along which they move as they wish, and caused to grow in it the varieties of plants from which come their food and the fodder of their animals. It is their origin from which they branched out, and their mother from whom they were born, and then it is their receptacle when they die [[His saying "then it is their receptacle when they die" means the place in which they are gathered. Related from al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari). (ع)]]. For this reason the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Rub yourselves with the earth, for it is kind to you" (ﷺ) [[Related by Ibn Abi Shaybah from ʿUlayyah from ʿAwf from Ibn ʿUthman, as a mursal report. It was also related by al-Tabarani in al-Saghir from the narration of al-Firyabi from al-Thawri from ʿAwf, and it was connected by mentioning Sulayman. Ibn Tahir said: the mursal version is closer to the correct one.]].

Ara'nahu: we showed him (bi-basarnāhu, "we made him see it") or we made him know it, its truth, and made him certain of it by it. He denied it only because of his wrongdoing (zulm), as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [27:14], and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿You know well that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs﴾ [17:102].

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿all Our signs﴾ (āyātinā kullahā), there are two interpretations. The first: this annexed definite form (al-ta'rīf al-iḍāfī) is treated like the definite form with the article (al-ta'rīf bi-l-lām), as if it had been said "al-āyāt kulluhā" (all the signs), meaning that it gives only the definiteness of reference ('ahd), pointing to the well-known signs, which are the nine signs specific to Moses, peace be upon him: the staff, the hand, the splitting of the sea, the stone, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the lifting of the mountain (naṭq al-jabal). The second: Moses had shown him his signs and enumerated for him what other prophets were given of their signs and miracles, and he was a truthful prophet, with no difference between what he reports and what he displays as evidence; so he denied them all and refused to accept any of them. It has also been said: he denied the signs and refused to accept the truth.

It appears from the tone of his words, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your sorcery?", that his limbs were trembling with fear of what Musa (عليه السلام) had brought, because he knew and was certain that he was upon the truth, and that one who is in the right, if he wished to pull the mountains, they would yield to him, and that one such as him is not forsaken and his helper does not fall short, and that he would certainly overcome him in his kingdom. His saying "with your sorcery" is an excuse and a bewildered pretext, for otherwise how could it be hidden from him that a sorcerer cannot drive out a king like himself from his land and overpower his kingdom by sorcery?

The choice of "appointment" (al-mawʿid) in His words ﴿فَاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِدًا﴾ ("So appoint between us and you a meeting place") must be one of three: it may be a time, a place, or a verbal noun (maṣdar). If you take it as a time, two problems arise. First, His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ ("Your appointment is the Day of Adornment") must match it. This requires you to make the time a [[Ahmad's marginal note: Mahmud said, "If you make the first appointment a noun of place, to match His words ﴿مَكَانًا سُوًى﴾ ("a place, equal"), you incur..." etc.]] and the verb governing the place becomes obstructed for you. If you take it as a place, to match His words ﴿مَكَانًا سُوًى﴾, you incur also that the appointment (the promise) is open to the breaking of the agreement regarding the place, and His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ do not match it. The reading of al-Hasan (al-Basri) does not match it in either place or time, because he read ﴿يَوْمَ الزِّينَةِ﴾ in the accusative. So what remains is to take it as a verbal noun in the sense of a promise, and to posit an omitted genitive construction, meaning "a place of appointment," and to take the pronoun in ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾ as referring to the appointment, with ﴿مَكَانًا﴾ as a substitute (badal) for the omitted place.

If you say: how does His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ﴾ then match the answer, when you must take it as a time, while the question concerns a place and not a time? I say: it matches in meaning though not in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment in a specific place, well known for their gathering there on that day; so by mentioning the time the place is known.

As for al-Hasan's reading, the appointment there is a verbal noun only: the meaning is "the fulfilment of your promise on the Day of Adornment." The matching of this is also by way of meaning.

It is also permissible not to posit an omitted genitive, and the meaning is: "Make between us and you a promise which we will not break." If you say: then in what is ﴿مَكَانًا﴾ in the accusative? I say: it is governed by the verbal noun, or by a verb indicated by the verbal noun. If you say: then how does the answer match it? I say: on al-Hasan's reading it is clear; on the common reading it is on the assumption: "Your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment."

It is permissible on al-Hasan's reading that ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ be the subject (mubtada'), in the sense of "the time," and ﴿ضُحًى﴾ its predicate, with the definiteness intended in it, because it is the forenoon of that very day. It has been said that the Day of Adornment was the Day of ʿAshura', the Day of Nayrudh (Nowruz) [the editor's note: the text reads "al-Nayrudh," probably meaning al-Nayrouz with a z, as in other versions], a festival that they held every year, a day on which they would set up a market and adorn themselves. ﴿نُخْلِفُهُ﴾ was read with a nominative ending (ḍamma), as a description of the appointment, and with a jussive ending, as an answer to the imperative. ﴿سُوًى﴾ was read as ﴿سُوًى﴾ and ﴿سُوَى﴾ with kasra and with damma, and with tanwin and without tanwin. Its meaning: "equitable between us and you," according to Mujahid, and it derives from "istiwa'" (evenness), because the distance from the middle to both ends is even, with no disparity. As for whoever reads without tanwin, the reasoning is that pausal form is applied to the continuous speech.

It was read ﴿وَأَنْ يُحْشَرَ النَّاسُ﴾ with the letter ta' and with ya'. The meaning with ta': "and that you, O Pharaoh, be gathered"; "and that the day be gathered." It is permissible that the pronoun of Pharaoh be in it, and he is referred to with the third person by the usual custom of addressing kings, or he addressed the people by His words ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ﴾ and made ﴿يُحْشَرَ﴾ refer to Pharaoh. The position of ﴿أَنْ يُحْشَرَ﴾ is nominative or genitive, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the day" or "the adornment."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 62–64:

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "Their secret counsel" means: "If Musa overcomes us, we will follow him." And on the authority of Qatada: "If he is a sorcerer, we will overcome him; and if he is from the heaven, then there is a command concerning him." And on the authority of Wahb: when [Musa] said, ﴿Woe to you...﴾ [the verse], they said: "This is not the word of a sorcerer."

The apparent meaning is that they consulted in secret and tugged at the edges of speech (tajadhabu ahdab al-qawl), then said: ﴿Indeed, these two are surely sorcerers.﴾ Their secret counsel was therefore in fabricating and forging this speech, out of fear of being overcome by the two of them, and in discouraging the people from following them.

Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ in the manifest, open manner. Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadha lasahirani﴾, according to the form "inna Zayd la-munṭaliq" (indeed Zayd is surely departing). The lam is what distinguishes the negating inna from the light form of the heavy inna.

Ubayy recited: ﴿inna dhani illa sahirani﴾. Ibn Masʿud recited: ﴿anna hadhani sahiran﴾, with anna pronounced with a fatha and without the lam, in apposition to the secret counsel (al-najwa).

It has been said that the well-known reading ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, who treated the dual noun like the nouns ending in alif, such as ʿasa (staff) and Saʿda, so they did not convert the alif into yaʾ in the genitive and accusative cases. Some of them said: inna here means "nam" (yes), and ﴿la-sahiran﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, with the lam entering upon the whole sentence, its estimated sense being: "for them are two sorcerers." Abu Ishaq was impressed by this view.

They called their doctrine "the best way" (al-tariqa al-muthla) and "the excellent custom" (al-sunna al-fudhla), and "every party rejoices in what it has" (kullu hizbin bima ladayhim farihun). It has been said: they meant the people of their best way, namely the Children of Israel, on the basis of Musa's words, ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel.﴾ It has also been said that "the way" (al-tariqa) is a term for the notables and leaders of the people, who serve as models for others; it is said: "They are the way of their people," and it is also said of one person: "He is the way of his people."

﴿So gather your plot﴾ is supported by His words, ﴿then he gathered his plot﴾. It was also read ﴿fa-ajmiʿu kaydakum﴾, meaning: resolve upon it and make it a matter agreed upon, so that you do not disagree and no one among you holds back from it, like a matter on which there is consensus.

They were commanded to come in a row (saffan), because it is more awe-inspiring in the hearts of those who see. It is related that they were seventy thousand, each one with a rope and a staff, and they came forward in a single advance. On the authority of Abu ʿUbayda, he interpreted the row (al-saff) as the place of prayer, because people gather there for their festival and prayers, lined up in rows. Its soundness lies in its being used as a proper name for a particular place of prayer, so they were commanded to come to it. Or it is intended: come to one of the places of prayer.

﴿And today he has indeed prospered who prevails﴾ is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ). That is: and indeed he who overcomes has succeeded.

Anna with what follows it is either governed by a suppressed verb, or it is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The meaning is: choose one of the two options, or the matter is your throwing or our throwing.

This offering of choice from them is a fine display of courtesy toward him, humility, and lowering of the wing, and it is also a sign that they were giving him fairness from themselves. [[Mahmud said: "God inspired them with good manners toward Moses, peace be upon him, in giving him the choice and in giving fairness from themselves." Ahmad said: Before that they had already behaved courteously toward him with their words ﴿So set for us an appointment, which neither we nor you shall fail to keep﴾ (20:58), leaving the setting of the appointment to him. Just as God, mighty and majestic, inspired Moses here to let them begin with what they had, so that his throwing of the staff after theirs would be "a truth cast against falsehood, which crushes it, and so it vanishes" (21:18), so too He inspired him at the outset to make their appointment the day of their adornment and their gathering, so that the truth would be manifest before the assembled witnesses, which would make their scheming more exposed and the veil over their shame more torn away. God knows best.]] It seems that God, mighty and majestic, inspired them with this, and that Moses, may God's blessings be upon him, knew whether they would choose to throw first or not. This was a matter of answering courtesy with courtesy, so that they would bring forth everything they had of magical plots and exhaust their utmost strength and effort. When they did so, God displayed His authority, cast the truth against falsehood so that it crushed it, and set the miracle upon the magic so that it destroyed it. It became a clear sign to those who look and a manifest lesson to those who take heed.

It is said of this ﴿idha﴾ that it is idha al-mufaja'a (the "sudden-surprise" idha). The precise analysis is that it is the idha which means "the time," which requires a governing element and a clause as its complement. In some contexts it is restricted to having as its governing element a particular verb, namely the verb of surprise, and the clause that follows is only a beginning clause (a nominal clause). So the construction of God's words ﴿fa-idha hibaluhum wa-'isiyyuhum﴾ is: Moses was surprised at the time of imagining their ropes and staffs. This is a representation. The meaning is: at his being surprised by their ropes and staffs, which were imagined to him as moving.

ʿIṣiyyuhum (عِصِيُّهُمْ) is read with a ḍamma, which is the original form, and with a kasra, which is ittiba' (vowel assimilation to the following letter). A parallel is dalīy/dulī and qasīy/qisī. It is also read tukhayyalu (تُخَيَّلُ) with its verb attributed to the pronoun of the ropes and staffs, and the phrase ﴿annaha tas'a﴾ (that it was moving) stands as a substitute from the pronoun, a badal al-ishtimal (inclusion apposition), like your saying: "Zayd impressed me, his generosity." It is also read tukhayyalu on the basis that the ropes and staffs are the ones causing the imagining of their motion. Also read tatakhayyalu (تَتَخَيَّلُ), whose pattern is that of takhayyala. And it is read nukhayyilu (نُخَيِّلُ), on the basis that God, exalted is He, is the one who causes the imagining as a trial and a test. It is related that they had smeared them with mercury, and when the sun shone upon them they moved and shook, and so this was imagined.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 67–69:

"Ījās al-khawf" (the concealing of fear): concealing something of it. Likewise "tawajjus al-sawt" (perceiving a sound): hearing a faint sound from it. This was due to the natural disposition of human nature, and it is hardly possible to be free of its like. It is also said: he feared that doubt would creep into the people so they would not follow him.

﴿Verily, you are the one who prevails﴾: in it is an affirmation of his victory and dominance, and emphasis through the use of a resumptive construction (al-istinaf), the word of emphasis (inna), the repetition of the pronoun (anta), the definite article (al-), the word for height (al-'uluw), which means manifest dominance, and the superlative form.

His saying ﴿what is in your right hand﴾ and not "your staff" (ʿaṣāka): al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'what is in your right hand' and did not say 'your staff' ..." The Ahmad (commentator on al-Kashshaf, Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The intended purpose of belittling it in the face of power is to belittle the trickery of the sorcerers by a stronger way, because if it is greater than that [the sorcerers' trickery] and yet it is petty in the face of God's power, then what is to be thought of their trickery when this petty, insignificant thing has swallowed it? The eloquent have a method of exalting praise by magnifying the army of the enemy of the one being praised, so that it implies magnifying the army of the one praised, who has overcome and conquered it. So God diminished the matter of the staff, so that it implies diminishing the trickery of the sorcerers, which it annihilates in an instant.

It is permissible that this is a diminishing of it, meaning: do not care about the abundance of their ropes and staves, and throw the small, single, slight-bodied stick that is in your right hand, for by the power of God it will swallow them in their singleness and multiplicity, their smallness and their greatness.

It is also permissible that it is a magnifying of it, meaning: do not give importance to these large, numerous bodies, for in your right hand is something greater than all of them, and these, despite their number, are the least and most insignificant in its eyes, so throw it and it will swallow them by God's leave and annihilate them. ﴿Talqaf﴾ is read in the nominative as a resumptive clause, or as a circumstantial clause, meaning: throw it swallowing [them]. It is also read ﴿talaqqafu﴾ with the lightened form.

(Note: the gloss on the reading "talaqqafu" with lightened form is from the editor's notes.)

ṣanaʿū here means zawwarū (they fabricated) and iftaʿalū, as in His saying ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾ (taltaqifu mā yafikūn). ﴿Kayda sāḥirin﴾ is read in the nominative and accusative. Whoever reads it in the nominative, it is on the basis that "mā" is a relative pronoun. Whoever reads it in the accusative, it is on the basis that "mā" is a restrictive particle (kāffa). It is also read "kayda siḥrin," meaning: possessor of sorcery, or possessors of sorcery; or they, due to their deep immersion in sorcery, are as if they were sorcery itself in its very essence; or it is "between the trickery" [i.e., "by sorcery"], since it is sorcery and not-sorcery, as one says "the hundred is distinguished by dirhams." Similar to it: "knowledge of jurisprudence" and "knowledge of grammar." If you ask: why is "sāḥir" singular and not plural? I say: because the intent in this statement is the sense of genus, not the sense of number; had it been plural, it would have been understood that the intended meaning is number.

Do you not see His saying ﴿and the sorcerer does not prosper﴾, meaning this genus. If you ask: why is it indefinite first and definite second? I say: it is indefinite only because of the indefiniteness of the genitive construction, not because of indefiniteness in itself, like the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

The intended meaning is the indefiniteness of the matter, as if it were said: what they did is trickery of sorcery, and in a worldly striving, and a worldly and otherworldly matter, [i.e., of a kind] "wherever it comes from" (ḥaythu atā), like their saying: "whichever way it goes," "whichever path it takes," and "wherever it may be."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 67–69:

"Ījās al-khawf" (the concealing of fear): concealing something of it. Likewise "tawajjus al-sawt" (perceiving a sound): hearing a faint sound from it. This was due to the natural disposition of human nature, and it is hardly possible to be free of its like. It is also said: he feared that doubt would creep into the people so they would not follow him.

﴿Verily, you are the one who prevails﴾: in it is an affirmation of his victory and dominance, and emphasis through the use of a resumptive construction (al-istinaf), the word of emphasis (inna), the repetition of the pronoun (anta), the definite article (al-), the word for height (al-'uluw), which means manifest dominance, and the superlative form.

His saying ﴿what is in your right hand﴾ and not "your staff" (ʿaṣāka): al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'what is in your right hand' and did not say 'your staff' ..." The Ahmad (commentator on al-Kashshaf, Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The intended purpose of belittling it in the face of power is to belittle the trickery of the sorcerers by a stronger way, because if it is greater than that [the sorcerers' trickery] and yet it is petty in the face of God's power, then what is to be thought of their trickery when this petty, insignificant thing has swallowed it? The eloquent have a method of exalting praise by magnifying the army of the enemy of the one being praised, so that it implies magnifying the army of the one praised, who has overcome and conquered it. So God diminished the matter of the staff, so that it implies diminishing the trickery of the sorcerers, which it annihilates in an instant.

It is permissible that this is a diminishing of it, meaning: do not care about the abundance of their ropes and staves, and throw the small, single, slight-bodied stick that is in your right hand, for by the power of God it will swallow them in their singleness and multiplicity, their smallness and their greatness.

It is also permissible that it is a magnifying of it, meaning: do not give importance to these large, numerous bodies, for in your right hand is something greater than all of them, and these, despite their number, are the least and most insignificant in its eyes, so throw it and it will swallow them by God's leave and annihilate them. ﴿Talqaf﴾ is read in the nominative as a resumptive clause, or as a circumstantial clause, meaning: throw it swallowing [them]. It is also read ﴿talaqqafu﴾ with the lightened form.

(Note: the gloss on the reading "talaqqafu" with lightened form is from the editor's notes.)

ṣanaʿū here means zawwarū (they fabricated) and iftaʿalū, as in His saying ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾ (taltaqifu mā yafikūn). ﴿Kayda sāḥirin﴾ is read in the nominative and accusative. Whoever reads it in the nominative, it is on the basis that "mā" is a relative pronoun. Whoever reads it in the accusative, it is on the basis that "mā" is a restrictive particle (kāffa). It is also read "kayda siḥrin," meaning: possessor of sorcery, or possessors of sorcery; or they, due to their deep immersion in sorcery, are as if they were sorcery itself in its very essence; or it is "between the trickery" [i.e., "by sorcery"], since it is sorcery and not-sorcery, as one says "the hundred is distinguished by dirhams." Similar to it: "knowledge of jurisprudence" and "knowledge of grammar." If you ask: why is "sāḥir" singular and not plural? I say: because the intent in this statement is the sense of genus, not the sense of number; had it been plural, it would have been understood that the intended meaning is number.

Do you not see His saying ﴿and the sorcerer does not prosper﴾, meaning this genus. If you ask: why is it indefinite first and definite second? I say: it is indefinite only because of the indefiniteness of the genitive construction, not because of indefiniteness in itself, like the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

In a hadith of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Neither in a matter of this world nor in a matter of the next." The intended meaning is the indefiniteness of the matter, as if it were said: what they did is trickery of sorcery, and in a worldly striving, and a worldly and otherworldly matter, [i.e., of a kind] "wherever it comes from" (ḥaythu atā), like their saying: "whichever way it goes," "whichever path it takes," and "wherever it may be."

Glory be to God! How wondrous is their affair! They cast their ropes and staves in disbelief and denial, then an hour later they cast their heads down in gratitude and prostration. How great is the difference between the two castings!

[[Mahmud said: "Glory be to Him who made a distinction between the two castings: their casting of their ropes and staves..." etc. Ahmad said: In the repetition of the word "casting" and the departure from a phrase like "so the magicians prostrated," there is an awakening of the listener to the subtle kindness of God Most High in transferring His servants from the extreme of disbelief and obstinacy to the utmost of faith and rectitude. This awakening cannot be achieved in this manner for this purpose except by repeating a single word with two contradictory meanings. This fits what I mentioned earlier concerning the conciseness of address in His words ﴿And cast what is in your right hand﴾ [20:69] and ﴿and what is that in your right hand?﴾ [20:17]. So reflect upon it, for the truth is fine and harmonious, and God is the Granter of success.]]

It is narrated that they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their respective people. From Ikrimah: When they fell down prostrate, God showed them, in their prostration, their dwellings which they would come to in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 71:

"Surely he is your chief (kabirukum)" — i.e., your greatest (la'dhimukum). He means: he is the most skilled of them and the highest in rank in their craft. Or "your teacher" (mu'allimukum), from the saying of the people of Makkah to the teacher: "My chief (kabiri) commanded me," and "My chief (kabiri) said to me, such-and-such." They mean by it their teacher and master in the Qur'an and in everything.

It is recited as "fa-la-uqatti'anna" and "wa-la-usallibanna" with the light (takhfif) form. The cutting "min khilaf" means: the right hand is cut off together with the left leg, because each of the two limbs is opposite to the other, in that this is a hand and that is a leg, and this is the right side and that is the left. The "min" is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), because the cutting begins and arises from the opposition of one limb to the other, not from their agreement with each other. The place of the prepositional phrase is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., "I shall cut them off while they are differing," because when some of them oppose one another, they are characterized by difference.

He likened the firmness of the crucified one on the trunk to the firmness of a thing placed in its container, and therefore it was said "upon the trunks of palm trees" (fi juzu'i al-nakhl).

"Which of us (ayyuna)" means himself, may God curse him, and Musa, upon him be blessings from God, as is shown by his saying "you believed in him" (amantum lahu). The lam with the verb "to believe" (iman) in the Book of God is used for other than God the Exalted, as in His saying: "He believes in God and believes for the believers" (yu'minu lil-mu'minin). In it is arrogance [[His saying "wa-fihi nafājah" — in al-Sihah: "rajul nafmaj" when he is a man of pride and haughtiness. (Ayn?)]] in his power and dominance, and in what he was accustomed to and practiced: torturing people with various kinds of torment. It also belittles Musa, upon him be peace, and treats him as weak while mocking him, because Musa had never been involved in torture at all.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 72–76:

﴿وَالَّذِي فَطَرَنَا﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿مَا جَاءَنَا﴾ ("what has come to us"), or it is an oath (qasam). It has been read as ﴿تَقْضِي هَذِهِ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ ("you decree this worldly life"). Its justification in the well-known reading is that ﴿الْحَيَاةَ﴾ is in the accusative as a time adverb (ẓarf), but the usage was extended by treating the adverb as if it were a direct object (maf‘ūl bih), as when you say, regarding "I fasted the day of Friday" (ṣumtu yawm al-jumʿa), "ṣīma yawm al-jumʿa" (the day of Friday was fasted).

It is narrated that the sorcerers, meaning their leaders, numbered seventy-two: two of them were Copts, and the rest were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled them to learn magic. It is also narrated that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses while he sleeps," and he did so. They found his staff guarding him, so they said: "This is not the sorcery of a sorcerer, for when a sorcerer sleeps, his sorcery becomes void." But Pharaoh refused except that they should oppose him.

﴿تَزَكَّى﴾ means purified himself from the defilements of sins.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it means "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh).

Regarding these three verses, it has been said that they are a report of their words. It has also been said that they are a statement from God, not in the form of a quotation.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 20, verses 77–79:**

﴿فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقاً﴾ (So strike for them a path), meaning: make a path for them. This is from the Arab expression "ḍaraba lahu fī mālihi sahman" (he assigned him a share in his wealth), and "ḍaraba al-labana" (he made the milk, i.e. he prepared the bricks).

*Yabs* (dry, ﴿يَبَساً﴾) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a descriptive adjective. It is said: "yabisa yabsan wa yabsan" (it became dry). [[Mahmud said: "It is read with a sukūn on the bāʾ and with a fatḥa on it..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: There is another explanation, namely that the measure of each part of the path was itself a path. It was like this because there were twelve paths, one for each tribe. And God knows best.]] Similar to it are *ʿadam* and *ʿadam* (both meaning absence/lack). For this reason it is applied to the feminine, as in "shātunā yabs" (our ewe is dry) and "nāqatunā yabs" (our she-camel is dry), when her milk has dried up. It is also read as *yabsan* and *yābisan*.

The word *yabs* cannot be free of one of three possibilities: that it is a lightened form (mukhaffaf) of *yabs* (with a sukūn), or that it is an adjective of the pattern *fiʿl*, or that it is the plural of *yābis*, like *ṣāḥib* and *ṣaḥb*, used as a descriptive term for the singular for emphasis, as in the verse of the poet:

*...... wa maʿan jiyāʿan*

*Kaʾanna qutūda raḥlī ḥīna ḍummat*
*ḥawālība ghurzan wa maʿan jiyāʿan*
*ʿalā waḥshiyyatin khudhilat khalūjun*
*wa kāna lahā ṭalāʾun ṭiflun fa-ḍāʿa*
*fakarrat tabtaghīhi fa-ṣādafathu*
*ʿalā damihi wa maṣraʿihi al-sibāʿā*

This is by al-Quṭāmī in praise of Zufar ibn al-Ḥārith al-Kilābī. *Al-qutūd* are the sticks of the saddle, plural of *aqtād*, plural of *qatad*. *Al-ḥawālibān* are two veins flanking the navel. *Al-ghuruz* is the plural of *gharīz* (with the rāʾ placed before the zāy), meaning those with little milk, the opposite of *al-ghazar* (with the zāy placed before the rāʾ). *Al-maʿiyy* is the passage of food in the belly among the intestines. He described it with the plural form, *jiyāʿan* (hungry), as hyperbole. The meaning is "hungry" (singular), and this is a metaphor for the emaciation of the she-camel from the intensity of travel, and it contains an allusion to the poverty and destitution of the rider. *ʿAlā waḥshiyyatin* is the predicate of *kāna*. *Al-waḥshiyya* is the female gazelle. *Khudhilat* is her description, i.e. the herd of gazelles abandoned her. *Khalūj* is another description; *khalaja* and *ikhtalaja* mean to be agitated and to go away, and *khalajahu* and *ikhtalajahu* mean to snatch and pull him away. *Al-khalūj* is the one whose young has been snatched from her, among gazelles or camels, or the one whose heart is agitated due to not seeing it. *Al-ṭalāʾ* is the young of a gazelle or similar cloven-hoofed animal. *Ṭifl* means small. *Fakarrat* means she returned quickly seeking it. *Al-sibāʿ* is a substitute of a transitional (idrāb intiqālī) relation from the pronoun in *ṣādafathu*, or it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb indicated by *ṣādafathu*, meaning: she encountered the predators standing over its blood and its place of falling, i.e. the place where it was thrown on the ground. He likened the she-camel to her in that state for her swiftness and alertness, and made it (the she-camel) as hungry as a group of hungry ones because of her excessive hunger.

﴿لا تَخافُ﴾ (you shall not fear) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in *fāḍrib*. It is also read *lā takhaf* (you shall not fear), as an answer (jawāb) to a command. Abū Ḥaywa read ﴿دَرَكاً﴾ with a sukūn. *Al-darak* and *al-darak* are both nouns from *al-idrāk* (overtaking), meaning: Pharaoh and his troops shall not overtake you, and they shall not reach you.

Regarding ﴿وَلا تَخْشى﴾ (nor shall you be afraid), when it is read as *lā takhaf*, there are three possibilities: that it is a new clause (istiʾnāf), as if it were said "and you do not fear," meaning: it is part of your nature that you are secure and do not fear. Or that the alif is not the one converted from a yāʾ which is the third radical of the verb, but is an extra alif added for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila), like the verses ﴿فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا﴾ (they led us astray from the way) and ﴿وَتَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ الظُّنُونَا﴾ (and you assumed about God assumptions). Or it is similar to the verse of the poet:

*Wa tiḍḥaku minnī shaykhatun ʿabshamiyyatun*
*kaʾan lam tara qablī asīran yamāniyyā*
*Wa ẓalla nisāʾu al-ḥayyi ḥawlī rukadan*
*yurāwidnanī mā turīdu nisāʾiyā*

These are by ʿAbd Yaghūth ibn Waqqāṣ al-Ḥārithī, who was captured on the day of al-Kilāb among the Banū Tamīm, and he composed a poem mentioning his condition in which he was. *Al-shaykha* is the old woman. *Al-ʿabshamiyya* means one attributed to ʿAbd Shams; it is a form of coinage (naḥt). He retained the alif in *tara* although it is jussive, either for the necessity of the metre or as an expansion of the language. It was said that it is the radical of the verb, and its original form is *tarāy*, whose final radical was dropped for the jussive, the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the rāʾ, and the fāʾ was replaced. The use of *lam* as an operator for the accusative is reported, and its non-operating use (ihmāl) is also reported. The analogical form for the relative adjective from *yaman* is *yamanī*, but they dropped one of the two yāʾs of the relative suffix and compensated for it with the alif. He was being led by a boy, and I asked him: "Who are you?" He said: "The lord of the people," so I laughed at him. *Al-rukad*, like *rukaʿ*, is the plural of *rākida*, meaning remaining and not leaving his presence. *Al-murāwada* is a reciprocal form (mufāʿala) from *rāda yarūdu*, when one seeks out the condition of a place searching for fertility; it is close in meaning to *arāda yurīdu*, meaning: they seek from me gently and by testing: "Shall I be pleased or not?" The thing that my women desire from me is intercourse.

﴿ما غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ (what covered them) is from the figure of brevity (bāb al-ikhtiṣār) and from the comprehensive expressions (jawāmiʿ al-kalim) which, though few in words, carry many meanings. That is: there covered them what no one knows the reality of except God. It is also read ﴿فَغَشاهُمْ مِنَ الْيَمِّ ما غَشاهُمْ﴾ (so the sea covered them with what covered them). *Al-taghshiya* means covering.

The subject of *ghashāhum* is either God, Glorified is He; or *mā ghashāhum* (what covered them); or Pharaoh, because he is the one who led his troops into ruin and was the cause of their destruction. The statement ﴿وَما هَدى﴾ (and he did not guide) is said as mockery of him in the words ﴿وَما أَهْدِيكُمْ إِلَّا سَبِيلَ الرَّشادِ﴾ (and I do not guide you except to the way of right direction). [[Mahmud said: "It is only said 'and he did not guide' as mockery of him." Ahmad said: If you say: mockery is to use an expression whose intended meaning is the opposite of its implication, like their saying "indeed you are the forbearing, the upright," while their aim is to describe him with the opposite of these two qualities. But God's statement ﴿وَما هَدى﴾ has as its content what actually happened, so it is then merely an information about his not guiding his people. I say: It is so, but the usage is like "Zayd did not guide ʿAmr," which establishes that Zayd is knowledgeable about the way of guidance and is himself guided, but he did not guide ʿAmr. And Pharaoh was the greatest of the misguided in himself, so how could it be imagined that he would guide others? The realization of this is: God's statement ﴿وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ﴾ (and Pharaoh led his people astray) is sufficient to inform of his not guiding them, together with his additional misguidance of them, for one who does not guide may not even mislead, so it would be sufficient. And when the sufficiency of the first in the information is established, the second must have a meaning other than that, namely mockery. And God knows best.]]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 20, verses 77–79:**

*...... wa maʿan jiyāʿan*

*Kaʾanna qutūda raḥlī ḥīna ḍummat*
*ḥawālība ghurzan wa maʿan jiyāʿan*
*ʿalā waḥshiyyatin khudhilat khalūjun*
*wa kāna lahā ṭalāʾun ṭiflun fa-ḍāʿa*
*fakarrat tabtaghīhi fa-ṣādafathu*
*ʿalā damihi wa maṣraʿihi al-sibāʿā*

He likened the she-camel to her in that state for her swiftness and alertness, and made it (the she-camel) as hungry as a group of hungry ones because of her excessive hunger.

﴿لا تَخافُ﴾ (you shall not fear) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in *fāḍrib*. It is also read *lā takhaf* (you shall not fear), as an answer (jawāb) to a command. Abū Ḥaywa read ﴿دَرَكاً﴾ with a sukūn. *Al-darak* and *al-darak* are both nouns from *al-idrāk* (overtaking), meaning: Pharaoh and his troops shall not overtake you, and they shall not reach you.

Regarding ﴿وَلا تَخْشى﴾ (nor shall you be afraid), when it is read as *lā takhaf*, there are three possibilities: that it is a new clause (istiʾnāf), as if it were said "and you do not fear," meaning: it is part of your nature that you are secure and do not fear. Or that the alif is not the one converted from a yāʾ which is the third radical of the verb, but is an extra alif added for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila), like the verses ﴿فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا﴾ (they led us astray from the way) and ﴿وَتَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ الظُّنُونَا﴾ (and you assumed about God assumptions). Or it is similar to the verse of the poet:

*Wa tiḍḥaku minnī shaykhatun ʿabshamiyyatun*
*kaʾan lam tara qablī asīran yamāniyyā*
*Wa ẓalla nisāʾu al-ḥayyi ḥawlī rukadan*
*yurāwidnanī mā turīdu nisāʾiyā*

These are by ʿAbd Yaghūth ibn Waqqāṣ al-Ḥārithī, who was captured on the day of al-Kilāb among the Banū Tamīm, and he composed a poem mentioning his condition in which he was. *Al-shaykha* is the old woman. *Al-ʿabshamiyya* means one attributed to ʿAbd Shams; it is a form of coinage (naḥt). He retained the alif in *tara* although it is jussive, either for the necessity of the metre or as an expansion of the language. It was said that it is the radical of the verb, and its original form is *tarāy*, whose final radical was dropped for the jussive, the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the rāʾ, and the fāʾ was replaced. The analogical form for the relative adjective from *yaman* is *yamanī*, but they dropped one of the two yāʾs of the relative suffix and compensated for it with the alif. He said: "The lord of the people," so I laughed at him. *Al-rukad*, like *rukaʿ*, is the plural of *rākida*, meaning remaining and not leaving his presence. *Al-murāwada* is a reciprocal form (mufāʿala) from *rāda yarūdu*, when one seeks out the condition of a place searching for fertility; it is close in meaning to *arāda yurīdu*, meaning: they seek from me gently and by testing: "Shall I be pleased or not?" The statement ﴿وَما هَدى﴾ (and he did not guide) is said as mockery of him in the words ﴿وَما أَهْدِيكُمْ إِلَّا سَبِيلَ الرَّشادِ﴾ (and I do not guide you except to the way of right direction). [[Mahmud said: "It is only said 'and he did not guide' as mockery of him." Ahmad said: If you say: mockery is to use an expression whose intended meaning is the opposite of its implication, like their saying "indeed you are the forbearing, the upright," while their aim is to describe him with the opposite of these two qualities. But God's statement ﴿وَما هَدى﴾ has as its content what actually happened, so it is then merely an information about his not guiding his people. I say: It is so, but the usage is like "Zayd did not guide ʿAmr," which establishes that Zayd is knowledgeable about the way of guidance and is himself guided, but he did not guide ʿAmr. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 80–81:

"O Children of Israel" is an address to them after their deliverance from the sea and the destruction of the people of Pharaoh. It has also been said that it is addressed to those among them who were alive in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that God bestowed favour upon them through what He did for their forefathers. The first view is the sounder one. The meaning is: "We said, O Children of Israel," and the omission of the verb of saying (al-qawl) is common in the Qur'an.

It has been read as "anjaytukum" (I delivered you) and "razaqtukum" (I provided for you), and in the form of a promise and mutual appointment (wa'd and mu'ada). It has been read "al-ayman" in the genitive (al-jarr) by way of proximity (al-jiwar), as in the phrase "juhr dabb kharib" (the hole of a lizard, ruined). [Note: the grammatical gloss "al-jiwar" means assigning a word the case of a neighbouring word.]

He reminds them of the blessing of their deliverance and the destruction of their enemy, and of what Moses (peace be upon him) was promised: the secret conversation at the side of Mount Sinai, and the writing of the Torah on the tablets. The promise is attributed to them ("ila-hum") because it concerned them and was connected to them, since it was made to their prophet and their chiefs (nuqaba'), and its benefits returned to them, by which their religion and their law were sustained, and it included the rest of His blessings and provisions that He poured out upon them.

Their transgression in the matter of blessings is that they exceed the bounds of God regarding them: by disbelieving in them, by being distracted by amusement and luxury from giving thanks for them, by spending them in acts of disobedience, by withholding the rights of the poor from them, by being extravagant in spending them, and by being insolent, boastful and arrogant with them.

"Fa-yahilla" has been read, and from Ibn Mas'ud: "la yahillanna" [the reading is attested with the verb in the form that is read as "yahlul"]. [Note from the editor: the author's statement, "fa-yahilla" is the commonly known reading; and "man yahlil" with kasra. The reading "la yahillanna" should be clarified as to whether it is with kasra or damma.]

"And whoever incurs My wrath (yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi)": the form with kasra carries the sense of obligation, from "hall al-dayn yahillu" when its payment becomes due. From it is His saying, exalted is He, "until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice" (hatta yablugha al-hadyu mahillahu). The form with damma carries the sense of descending.

"The wrath of God" means His punishments. [Commentary note: Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Wrath is the punishment of God, exalted is He, upon them..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: he cannot take wrath to mean anything but punishment, because it negates the attribute of will among the attributes of perfection that he negates. But according to the principle of the Sunnah it is permissible that the intended meaning of wrath is the will to punish, so it would be among the attributes of the Essence. It is also possible that it means treating them as one treats someone whom one has observed to be wrathful, so it would be among the attributes of acts. As for describing Him as "descending" (hulul), it cannot be taken to mean will, and it is like His statement, upon him be prayer and peace, "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven," according to the well-known interpretation (ta'wil). Or it expresses the descent of the effect of the will by the descent of the will itself, expressing the effect by its cause, as one who looks upon a marvel of God's creation says: "Look at the power of God," meaning the effect of power and not power itself. And God knows best.]

For this reason He is described with "fell" (hawa), meaning "perished." Its original meaning is to fall from a mountain and die.

[A poet] said:

"He fell from the top of a watch-post, and beneath it his liver was shattered."

[Another verse of the same poem:]

"My son fell from a lofty height, whose peak frightened its eagle,
He fell from the top of a watch-post, and beneath it his liver was shattered.
I am blamed for weeping over him, and I reach for him but do not find him,
And how is a grieving one blamed, bent, who has lost his son?"

[This is said by a Bedouin Arab (a'rabi) who says: my son fell from above a high mountain. Here "'ala" means "above" (fawqa). Had it been read "'ala" with damma, as the plural of "'aliyya" (a height), it would also be permissible, meaning he fell from the peaks of a high mountain. "Al-sharaf" is a verbal noun used as a figurative description (majaz). "Yahulu" means "frightens." "'Iqabuhu" means its height.

"Sa'ad" with kasra, "sa'dan" and "su'udan" with fatha and damma, means it rose up. The pronoun refers either to the eagle or to the height, so it is the verbal noun in an idafa to its subject. It is also permissible that it is in idafa to its object, meaning its ascent upon it. The eagle is singled out because it is the strongest of birds in ascending, especially the eagle of that mountain, which is known for it. "Hawa" is repeated to show grief, meaning he fell from the top of a high ridge where a sentinel keeps watch, and so his liver was torn beneath it, that is, beside it, so how much more the rest of his body. It is related as "fazat" with a shadda on the zay, meaning "he was frightened." It is also related as "farrat" with a shadda on the ra', originally "fariya," and this is the dialect of Tayy, who say "da'at" for "du'iyat" and "bunat" for "buniyat." Then he says: people blame me for weeping, though I touch him; from the pattern of "qatala" and "daraba," meaning I wish to touch him but do not find him. How is a grieving, aged man blamed, who has despaired of his son's return to him, or of the time of having more children?

It has been said that the speaker is the mother of the slain man, but the following verse is related before the first verse:

"No mother to weep for him, and no sister to miss him,
He fell from a hard rock, and beneath it his liver was shattered."

And so on to the end.]

And they say: "May his mother be bereaved (hawat ummuhu)." Or it means he fell a fall from which there is no rising again.

From it is His saying, exalted is He, "until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice" (hatta yablugha al-hadyu mahillahu). The form with damma carries the sense of descending.

"The wrath of God" means His punishments. [Commentary note: Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Wrath is the punishment of God, exalted is He, upon them..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: he cannot take wrath to mean anything but punishment, because it negates the attribute of will among the attributes of perfection that he negates. But according to the principle of the Sunnah it is permissible that the intended meaning of wrath is the will to punish, so it would be among the attributes of the Essence. It is also possible that it means treating them as one treats someone whom one has observed to be wrathful, so it would be among the attributes of acts. As for describing Him as "descending" (hulul), it cannot be taken to mean will, and it is like His statement, upon him be prayer and peace, "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven," according to the well-known interpretation (ta'wil). Or it expresses the descent of the effect of the will by the descent of the will itself, expressing the effect by its cause, as one who looks upon a marvel of God's creation says: "Look at the power of God," meaning the effect of power and not power itself. And God knows best.]

For this reason He is described with "fell" (hawa), meaning "perished." Its original meaning is to fall from a mountain and die.

[A poet] said:

"He fell from the top of a watch-post, and beneath it his liver was shattered."

[Another verse of the same poem:]

"My son fell from a lofty height, whose peak frightened its eagle,
He fell from the top of a watch-post, and beneath it his liver was shattered.
I am blamed for weeping over him, and I reach for him but do not find him,
And how is a grieving one blamed, bent, who has lost his son?"

[This is said by a Bedouin Arab (a'rabi) who says: my son fell from above a high mountain. Here "'ala" means "above" (fawqa). Had it been read "'ala" with damma, as the plural of "'aliyya" (a height), it would also be permissible, meaning he fell from the peaks of a high mountain. "Al-sharaf" is a verbal noun used as a figurative description (majaz). "Yahulu" means "frightens." "'Iqabuhu" means its height.

"Sa'ad" with kasra, "sa'dan" and "su'udan" with fatha and damma, means it rose up. The pronoun refers either to the eagle or to the height, so it is the verbal noun in an idafa to its subject. It is also permissible that it is in idafa to its object, meaning its ascent upon it. The eagle is singled out because it is the strongest of birds in ascending, especially the eagle of that mountain, which is known for it. "Hawa" is repeated to show grief, meaning he fell from the top of a high ridge where a sentinel keeps watch, and so his liver was torn beneath it, that is, beside it, so how much more the rest of his body. It is related as "fazat" with a shadda on the zay, meaning "he was frightened." It is also related as "farrat" with a shadda on the ra', originally "fariya," and this is the dialect of Tayy, who say "da'at" for "du'iyat" and "bunat" for "buniyat." Then he says: people blame me for weeping, though I touch him; from the pattern of "qatala" and "daraba," meaning I wish to touch him but do not find him. How is a grieving, aged man blamed, who has despaired of his son's return to him, or of the time of having more children?

It has been said that the speaker is the mother of the slain man, but the following verse is related before the first verse:

"No mother to weep for him, and no sister to miss him,
He fell from a hard rock, and beneath it his liver was shattered."

And so on to the end.]

And they say: "May his mother be bereaved (hawat ummuhu)." Or it means he fell a fall from which there is no rising again.

Guidance (al-ihtida'): this is steadfastness and firmness upon the guidance mentioned, which is repentance, faith and righteous deeds. Similar to it is the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast...﴾ [Qur'an 41:30]. The particle of delay (kalimat al-tarakhi, "then") indicates a difference between the two ranks, just as it indicates a difference between two times in "Zayd came to me, then 'Amr." I mean that the rank of steadfastness upon good is distinct from the rank of good itself, because it is higher than it and superior to it.

And what has made you hasten ahead of your people (﴿وَما أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ﴾), i.e. what caused you to hurry away from them? It is said in the form of disapproval. He had gone with the chosen leaders (al-nuqaba') to Mount Sinai at the appointed time. Then he went ahead of them, out of longing for the speech of his Lord and eagerness to fulfil what had been promised to him, based on his own reasoning and his assumption that this was closer to the pleasure of God, the Exalted. He overlooked that God, the Mighty and Majestic, does not fix the timing of His acts except in consideration of the motives of wisdom and with knowledge of the interests attached to each time. Therefore, by "the people" (al-qawm) are meant the leaders. The view of those who permit that the whole of his people be meant, and that he had left them before the appointed time, has no sound basis, since it is refuted by His saying ﴿هُمْ أُولاءِ عَلى أَثَرِي﴾ ("They are right behind me"). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿إثرى﴾ (ithri) with a kasra, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿أثرى﴾ (athri) with a damma.

Also from him (al-Zamakhshari's source, i.e. the reader): ﴿أولى﴾ (uli) is to be read with the short vowel. Al-ithr (إثر) is more eloquent than al-athr (أثر). As for al-athr, it is attested in the sense of the watered pattern on the blade of a sword (firind al-sayf), and it is recorded in the standard lexicons. It is said: ithr al-sayf and athruhu. Yet in the sense of "trace" the form ithr is rare.

If you say: "What has made you hasten ahead?" is a question about the cause of the haste, then the answer that fits it would be: "I sought to increase Your pleasure, or I yearned for Your speech and the fulfilment of Your promise." But His saying ﴿هُمْ أُولاءِ عَلى أَثَرِي﴾ is, as you see, not a fitting answer to it.

I say: what the Lord of Might confronted him with contained two things. The first: disapproval of the haste itself. The second: a question about the cause of what was disapproved and what prompted it. The more important of the two matters for Moses was to set out his excuse and to pave the way with a reason for what had been disapproved. So he argued that what had occurred from him was only a slight advance, which in custom is not counted or taken seriously, and that between me and the one who went before me there is only a short distance, such as a delegation's leader or head might advance by. Then he followed it with the answer to the question about the cause, saying ﴿وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضى﴾ ("And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased").

It may be said that he was bewildered by what came upon him of awe at the rebuke of God, and that this distracted him from an answer that fits and is ordered according to the limits of speech.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 85:

He meant by "the people who were tested" those whom he (Musa) had left behind with Harun, and they were six hundred thousand; of them, only twelve thousand did not escape worshipping the calf.

If you say: the story states that they remained for twenty nights after his departure, and they reckoned them as forty including their days, and said: "We have completed the appointed term." Then the matter of the calf came after that. So how is this reconciled with His saying, the Exalted, to Musa upon his arrival: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people after you﴾?

I say: Allah, the Exalted, has informed of the trial that was anticipated, using the wording of the trial that exists, in accordance with His practice. Or, as-Samiri seized the opportunity of his absence and resolved to lead them astray right after his departure, and began arranging that. Thus the beginning of the trial was already in existence.

It was read: ﴿And as-Samiri misled them﴾, meaning, while he was the most misguided of them, because he was misguided and misguiding. He is attributed to a tribe of the Children of Israel called as-Samirah. It was also said: as-Samirah are a people from among the Jews who differ with them in some of their religion. It was also said: he was from the people of Bajarma.

It was also said: he was a non-Arab man (ʿilj) from Kirman, named Musa ibn Zafar, and he was a hypocrite who had outwardly professed Islam, and he was from a people who worshipped cows.

Al-asaf: the very angry. From it is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying concerning sudden death: "It is a mercy for the believer and a seizing in anger (akhdhat asaf) for the disbeliever." [[Ahmad narrated it through ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr from ʿĀʾisha: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about sudden death" — and he mentioned it. It has another route in ʿAbd al-Razzaq, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), in which is Yahya ibn al-ʿAla al-Razi, who is weak. He and Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tabarani narrated it from their hadiths as a statement of ʿĀʾisha (mawquf). It is also reported as a statement of Ibn Masʿud (mawquf). On the subject there is a report from Anas in al-Janaʾiz of Ibn Shahin, and from ʿUbayd ibn Khalid in Abu Dawud with the wording "sudden death is a seizing in anger (akhdhat asaf)."]] It is also said: the grieving. If you ask: when did he return to his people? I answer: after he had completed the forty: Dhu al-Qaʿda and the ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. Allah promised them that He would give them the Torah, in which is guidance and light, and there is no promise better or finer than that. It has been related to us that it consisted of a thousand surahs, each surah of a thousand verses, and its volumes were carried by seventy camels.

Al-ʿahd: the time; he means the period of his separation from them. It is said: "My time (ʿahdi) with you has been long," meaning: my time has been long because of your separation. They had promised him that they would remain upon his command and the faith he had left them upon, but they broke their promise by worshipping the calf.

Bi-mulkina: it is read with the three vowel forms, meaning: we did not break our promise to you by our own power; had we had control of our affairs and been left to ourselves, we would not have broken it, but we were overcome from the side of the Samiri and his scheming.

That is: we carried loads of the ornaments of the Copts which we had borrowed from them. Or they meant by "burdens" that they were sins and consequences, because they were with them in the position of protected persons (mustaʾminun) in the abode of war, and it is not permissible for a protected person to take the property of a belligerent, especially since spoils were not lawful at that time.

Fa-qadhafnaha fi nar al-Samiri: the fire which he kindled in the pit, and we were commanded to throw the ornaments into it. It is also read "ḥamalna" (we carried).

Fa-kadhalika alqa al-Samiri: he showed them that he was throwing an ornament in his hand, like what they had thrown. He only threw the dust which he had taken from the hoof-print of Gabriel's horse. Satan inspired him that when it mixed with something dead, it would become an animal.

Fa-akhraja lahum al-Samiri min al-hufra ʿijlan: a calf created by Allah from the ornaments which the fire had melted, which lowed as calves low.

If you ask: how did that dust have an effect on bringing the dead to life? I answer: is it not valid that Allah, exalted is He, should favour the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) with this special honour, as He favoured him with other honours, namely that when he touched with his horse's hoof a dust, which then touched lifeless matter, Allah would bring into being, if He willed, an animal at his touch? Do you not see how He created Jesus without a father when He breathed into the garment?

If you ask: why did Allah create the calf from the ornaments, so that it became a trial for the Children of Israel and misguidance? I answer: this is not the first trial with which Allah tested His servants, so that Allah may make firm those who believed with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter, and Allah misguides the wrongdoers. It is strange that the calf was created, but the creation of Iblis is stranger still.

What is meant by His saying: "Indeed We have tried your people" is the creation of the calf as a test; that is, We tested them by creating the calf, and the Samiri led them into misguidance, and caused them to fall into it when he said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he has forgotten" — that is, Musa forgot to seek Him here, and went to seek Him at the Mount. Or "he forgot" refers to the Samiri: that is, he abandoned the outward faith he had been upon.

يَرْجِعُ (yarji'u) من رفعه فعلى أنّ أن (an) مخففة من الثقيلة (mukhaffafa min al-thaqila, the lightened form of the heavy *inna*). ومن نصب فعلى أنها الناصبة للأفعال (al-nasiba lil-af'al, the particle that puts verbs into the subjunctive) مِنْ قَبْلُ، أي من قبل أن يقول لهم السامري ما قال. كأنهم أوّل ما وقعت عليه أبصارهم حين طلع من الحفرة افتتنوا به واستحسنوه، فقبل أن ينطق السامري بادرهم هرون عليه السلام بقوله ﴿إِنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمنُ﴾.

"La" is redundant (*mazīda*, an extra particle with no separate meaning). The meaning is: "What prevented you from following me, out of zeal for God and strong opposition to unbelief and sins?"

"Why did you not fight those who disbelieved, rather than those who believed? And why did you not carry out the matter, as I would have done, had I been present?"

Or: "Why did you not follow me?"

Recited as "liḥyatī" (with a fatḥah on the lām): this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Mūsā, upon him be peace, was a man of quick temper, naturally inclined to hastiness, harshness and rigidity in everything, very fierce in his anger for God and His religion. When he saw his people worshipping a calf besides God after they had witnessed the great signs, he could not restrain himself: he threw down the tablets of the Torah, overcome by the great bewilderment that seized his mind, out of zeal for God, disdain and indignation. He treated harshly his brother and his deputy over his people, approaching him as an openly hostile enemy would, seizing him by the hair of his head—and he had a full head of hair—and by the hair of his beard, dragging him toward himself.

[Meaning:] If you had fought some of them against others, they would have scattered and destroyed one another; so I delayed, hoping that you yourself would take charge, mending matters with your own judgment. I feared your reproach for having abandoned what you had enjoined on me: to keep the community united and to protect the common folk, and I had no choice but to heed your charge and act upon its requirements.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verses 95–96:

Al-khatb (the matter, affair): a verbal noun from khataba al-amr, meaning he sought it. So when one says to someone who is doing something, "Ma khatbuka?", the meaning is: "What did you seek by it?"

It was read "baṣurtu bi-mā lam yabṣurū bihi" with a kasra (baṣurtu with kasra on the ta'), and the well-known reading is with a damma. It was also read "tabṣurū bihi" with the ta' (in the second person).

[[Note of the editor: al-Zamakhshari's words "and it was read baṣurtu bi-mā lam yabṣurū bihi with a kasra" — the well-known reading is with a damma. It was also read "tabṣurū bihi" with the ta'. The phrasing of al-Nasafi: "and with the ta' are Hamza and ʿAlī." It may have been dropped here inadvertently by the copyist; it should be verified. (ʿ)]]

The meaning: I knew what you did not know, and I perceived what you did not perceive.

Al-Hasan read "qabḍatan" with a damma on the qaf, and it is the name of the thing grasped, like "al-ghurfa" (a handful scooped) and "al-maḍgha" (a mouthful chewed). As for "al-qabḍa" (with a kasra), it denotes the single instance of grasping (qabḍ), and its use for the thing grasped is naming the object by the verbal noun, as in "ḍarb al-amīr" (the ruler's striking/the thing struck by the ruler's decree).

He also read "fa-qabaṣtu qabṣatan," with the unpointed ṣād. The ḍād (with the ḍād) is with the whole palm; the ṣād is with the fingertips. Similar to them are "al-khaḍm" and "al-qaḍm": the khā' is with the whole mouth, and the qāf is with its front part.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "min athari faras al-rasūl" (from the hoofprint of the horse of the Messenger).

If you ask: Why did he name him "the Messenger" and not Jibril or Ruh al-Qudus? I say: When the appointed time for going to Mount Sinai arrived, God sent Jibril to Musa, riding Ḥayzūm, the horse of life, to take him away. The Samiri saw him and said: "Surely this has a matter (of significance)," so he took a handful from the dust of the place where he trod. When Musa asked him about his story, he said: "I took it from the hoofprint of the one sent to you on the day the appointed time arrived." Perhaps he did not know that he was Jibril.

Ibn Mas'ud reports: "We will" – i.e., ﴿نَخْلِفَهُ﴾ with the nun (we will fail to fulfil it)...

Actually, the passage reads as follows:

He was punished in this world with a punishment more severe and more desolate than any other. He was forbidden from mixing with people altogether. They were prohibited from meeting him, speaking with him, trading with him, facing him, and from every form of dealing that people have with one another. If he happened to touch anyone, man or woman, both the one who touched and the one touched would be struck with fever. People shunned him and he shunned them, and he would cry out: "No touching" (﴿لَا مِسَاسَ﴾). Among people he became more desolate than the murderer who seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct, or the wild beast that flees into the desert. It is said that his people still follow this practice today. It has also been read as ﴿لَا مِسَاسَ﴾ with the pattern of فِجَار (fijār).

A similar expression is the saying about gazelles: "When they reach the water, there is no ʿabāb; and if they fail to find it, there is no abāb." These are names for the single instance of the verb ʿabba (to drink in one gulp), and abba (to seek/desire), where the form denotes a single occurrence of abb (seeking).

﴿لَن تُخْلَفَهُ﴾: meaning, God will not fail you in the promise He made you concerning your polytheism and corruption on earth; He will fulfil it for you in the Hereafter after having punished you for it in this world. Thus you are among those who have lost both this world and the Hereafter: ﴿ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْخُسْرَانُ الْمُبِينُ﴾ (That is the manifest loss). It has also been read as ﴿لَنْ تُخْلِفَهُ﴾, from the form أَخْلَفْتُ الْمَوْعِدَ (I found the appointment unfulfilled, i.e., I found it failed), when one finds that the promise has not been kept. al-A'sha said:

"He stayed, and shortened his night to provide for himself, then departed, and found Qutayla's appointment unfulfilled."

"He went on his errand, and his rope became worn out, while he had been in a state in which he would never be troubled."

This is by al-A'sha. Aqṣara ʿan al-shayʾ means he desisted from it and refrained from it; aqṣarahu means he found it short. It is reported as qaṣṣara (with doubled ṣād), and "laylahu" is reported with a pronoun suffix, but in al-A'sha's Dīwān it reads "laylatan" with a tā' marbūṭa. Thawā bi'l-makān means he stayed at the place, and athwā bihi is a dialectal variant of it, which can also be used transitively. He means: he cut short the journey and stayed at the abode of Qutayla, and found his night short, either because she visited him with union, or he refrained from travelling for that reason. The night passed in the first reading, or the night-time passed in the second. The solidity of the meaning supports this.

He found Qutayla's appointment unfulfilled, meaning he found it failing, so he set out on his journey as before. He used the image of the rope for affection, or for hope in it, by way of the metaphor of explicit comparison (al-tasrīḥiyya), and the element of "khalq" (worn out) is a supporting element (tarshīḥ). That is, he despaired of her affection, and the rope or the lover was in a good condition, namely that it would never be troubled, i.e., would never be disturbed, never be distressed, and its affair would never be made difficult. The loss of a blessing after obtaining it is hard on the soul. Khalq, with a ḍammah, is khulq, like ḥusn, and it is originally a verbal noun. Yankad is like yataʿab (to be weary).

From Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿نَخْلِفَهُ﴾ with the nūn, meaning God will not fail it. It is as though he related the words of the Mighty and Majestic, as has already been mentioned in ﴿لِأَهَبَ لَكِ﴾ (19:19).

﴿ظَلْتَ﴾ and ﴿ظلت﴾ are both read; the original is ﴿ظَلِلْتَ﴾, so they removed the first lām and transferred its vowel to the ẓāʾ. Some did not transfer it. ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ and ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ are read (both forms). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿لَنَذْبَحَنَّهُ﴾ and ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾. The two readings are from al-iḥrāq (burning). Abu ʿAli al-Fārisi mentioned that in ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ﴾ it is possible that ḥarraqa is an intensive form of ḥaraqa when it is filed down with a file. The third reading is upon it, and it is the reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: ﴿لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ﴾, with a kasra and a ḍammah on the sīn. This is a third punishment, namely the annulment of what he was tempted by and tempted others with, the wasting of his efforts, and the destruction of his scheming: ﴿وَمَكَرُوا وَمَكَرَ اللَّهُ وَاللَّهُ خَيْرُ الْمَاكِرِينَ﴾ (They schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers).

Talhah recited: "Allah, there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Lord of the Throne, He has encompassed (wasi'a) every thing in knowledge (ʿilman)." It is also reported from Mujahid and Qatadah: "wasa'a" (with fatha on the sin, i.e. the reading "wasa'a" in the form that makes it transitive). Its explanation: wasi'a (in the sense of "to encompass") is transitive to one object, which is "kull shay'" (every thing). As for ʿilman, its accusative case is that of tamyiz (specification), and in meaning it is the subject (fa'il). So when the verb became heavy, it was transferred to transitivity with two objects, and both were put in the accusative together as objects, because the tamyiz is the subject in meaning, just as you say in "khafa Zayd ʿAmran" (Zayd feared ʿAmr): "khawwaftu Zaydan ʿAmran" (I made Zayd fear ʿAmr). Thus by transference (naql) what was the subject becomes the object.

The kaf in ﴿kadhalika﴾ is in the accusative position (manṣūb al-maḥall), and this is a promise from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to His Messenger (ﷺ). That is: like that recounting, and like what We have recounted to you of the story of Musa and Fir'awn, We will relate to you from the rest of the reports of past nations, their stories and their conditions, to multiply your clear proofs and increase your miracles, so that the listener may take heed, the one seeking insight may gain greater insight into his religion, and the proof may be confirmed against him who obstinately opposes and is arrogant. And this Reminder which We have given you, meaning the Qur'an, containing these tales and reports which deserve reflection and consideration, is ﴿a mighty Reminder and a noble Qur'an﴾, in which there is salvation and happiness for whoever turns to it, while whoever turns away from it has perished and become wretched.

By "al-wizr" he means a heavy, crushing punishment. He called it a wizr (burden) by way of likening its weight upon the one punished, and the difficulty of bearing it, to a load that weighs down the bearer (yafdaḥu al-ḥāmil, "it weighs heavily upon the carrier") and breaks his back, and overpowers him (wa yulqā ʿalayhi bahruhu, "and overwhelms him"). [[The author's phrase "yafdaḥu al-ḥāmil" means: weighs down the carrier. Cited from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] [[The author's phrase "bahruhu" means: his overpowering. Cited from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] Or it is called a burden because it is the recompense of the wizr, which is sin.

It is also read as yaḥmilu (with the verb in the singular form). The plural ﴿khālidīna﴾ is used according to the meaning, because "man" (whoever) is a conditional that covers many, not a single person. The singular pronoun in ﴿aʿraḍa﴾ and what follows it is used according to the wording (of man). A similar example is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾.

﴿fīhi﴾ means: in that burden, or in bearing it.

﴿sāʾa﴾ is in the sense of ﴿bi'sa﴾ (evil is). The pronoun in it must be undefined (mubham), explained by ﴿ḥimlan﴾ (as a load). The object of the dispraise is omitted, because the preceding word ﴿wizr﴾ indicates it. Its estimate is: "Evil is the load their burden," just as it is omitted in the words of the Exalted: ﴿How excellent a servant; indeed he was one who turned back in repentance﴾, where Ayyub is the one praised. Similarly is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And evil is the destination﴾, meaning: "And evil is the destination, Hell."

If you ask: what is the lam in ﴿lahum﴾, and what does it relate to? I say: it is for clarification (lil-bayān), as in ﴿hayta laka﴾ (Come, you).

If you ask: why do you deny that the pronoun in ﴿sāʾa﴾ refers to the wizr? I say: it is not valid that the pronoun in ﴿sāʾa﴾ be the wizr, since its rule is the rule of ﴿bi'sa﴾, which is a pronoun for a specific thing, not an undefined one.

If you say: then let ﴿sāʾa﴾ not have the rule of ﴿bi'sa﴾, and let it be like the ﴿sāʾa﴾ in the words of the Exalted, ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be evil [sīʾat]﴾, in the sense of "to grieve and sadden"? I say: what is enough to prevent you from this is that it would turn the speech of Allah into your saying: "The wizr grieved them as a load on the Day of Resurrection," and that is after you have escaped the obligation of this lam and the obligation of this accusative.

The attribution of the blowing to Him, the One who commands, is in the reading of one who recites "nanfukh" with a nūn (Qur'an 20:102). Or it is because the honoured angels, and Isrāfīl among them, hold the rank they hold with the Lord of Might. So, because of their honour and nearness to Him, it is proper to attribute what they carry out to His own Essence, exalted is He. It is also recited as "yunfakh," in the form of the verb whose subject is not named, and as "yanfukh." And "yuḥshar," with an open yā' in the third person, where the pronoun refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, or to Isrāfīl, peace be upon him. As for "yuḥsharu al-mujrimūn" (the criminals are gathered), no one recited it except al-Ḥasan.

It is recited "fī al-ṣuwari" with a fatḥa on the wāw, as the plural of "ṣūra" (form). Regarding "fī al-Ṣūr" there are two opinions. The first is that it means the Ṣūr, and this recitation points to it. The second is that it means the horn (qarn). Regarding "zurq" (blue-eyed, Qur'an 20:102) there are two opinions. The first is that blueness was the most hateful of eye colours to the Arabs, because the Romans, their enemies, had blue eyes, and for this reason they described the enemy by saying: "black-livered, reddish-bearded, blue-eyed." The second is that what is meant is blindness, because the pupil of one whose sight has gone turns blue.

﴿They will speak in low voices among themselves﴾ (Qur'an 20:103), because of the fear and terror that fill their breasts. They will regard the length of their stay in the world as short. This is either because of the hardships they witness, which remind them of the days of blessing and joy, so they grieve over them and describe them as brief, since days of joy are short; or because those days have gone from them and come to an end, and what has gone, however long its duration, is short by its ending. From this is the note of Abdullah ibn al-Mu'tazz written beneath "may God prolong your life": "Ending is enough to make it short." Or it is because they consider the Hereafter long, as it is an everlasting eternity, so the lifespan of the world seems short in comparison, and it is said that the dwelling of its people in it is measured against their dwelling in the Hereafter.

God has preferred the saying of the one who is most precise among them in the words of His Exalted saying: ﴿When the best of them in conduct says: "You stayed only a day"﴾ (Qur'an 20:104), and a similar verse is His saying: ﴿He said: "How long did you remain on the earth, counting years?" They said: "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count."﴾ (Qur'an 23:112–113). It is also said that what is meant is their stay in the graves. This is supported by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will swear that they stayed no longer than an hour; thus they were deluded﴾ (Qur'an 30:55), and His saying: ﴿But those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You remained in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ (Qur'an 30:56).

And "yuḥshar," with an open yā' in the third person, where the pronoun refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, or to Isrāfīl, peace be upon him. As for "yuḥsharu al-mujrimūn" (the criminals are gathered), no one recited it except al-Ḥasan.

It is recited "fī al-ṣuwari" with a fatḥa on the wāw, as the plural of "ṣūra" (form). Regarding "fī al-Ṣūr" there are two opinions. The first is that it means the Ṣūr, and this recitation points to it. The second is that it means the horn (qarn). Regarding "zurq" (blue-eyed, Qur'an 20:102) there are two opinions. The first is that blueness was the most hateful of eye colours to the Arabs, because the Romans, their enemies, had blue eyes, and for this reason they described the enemy by saying: "black-livered, reddish-bearded, blue-eyed." The second is that what is meant is blindness, because the pupil of one whose sight has gone turns blue.

﴿They will speak in low voices among themselves﴾ (Qur'an 20:103), because of the fear and terror that fill their breasts. They will regard the length of their stay in the world as short. This is either because of the hardships they witness, which remind them of the days of blessing and joy, so they grieve over them and describe them as brief, since days of joy are short; or because those days have gone from them and come to an end, and what has gone, however long its duration, is short by its ending. From this is the note of Abdullah ibn al-Mu'tazz written beneath "may God prolong your life": "Ending is enough to make it short." Or it is because they consider the Hereafter long, as it is an everlasting eternity, so the lifespan of the world seems short in comparison, and it is said that the dwelling of its people in it is measured against their dwelling in the Hereafter.

God has preferred the saying of the one who is most precise among them in the words of His Exalted saying: ﴿When the best of them in conduct says: "You stayed only a day"﴾ (Qur'an 20:104), and a similar verse is His saying: ﴿He said: "How long did you remain on the earth, counting years?" They said: "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count."﴾ (Qur'an 23:112–113). It is also said that what is meant is their stay in the graves. This is supported by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will swear that they stayed no longer than an hour; thus they were deluded﴾ (Qur'an 30:55), and His saying: ﴿But those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You remained in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ (Qur'an 30:56).
