He reduces it to sand, then sends winds upon it that scatter it as grain is winnowed. ﴿So He will leave it as a level plain﴾ [[The commentary on His words, ﴿leave it as a level plain﴾, in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari): both al-Qaa' (level ground) and al-Safsaf mean a flat expanse of land, so al-Safsaf is an emphatic reinforcement. (ʿAyn)]], that is, He will leave its places of settlement and its centres. Or the pronoun may refer to the earth, though it has not been mentioned, as in His words: ﴿He left upon its back not a single creature﴾.

If you say: they distinguished between ʿiwaj (العوج) and ʿawaj (العوج), saying that ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for abstract meanings and ʿawaj with a fatha is used for concrete objects, and the earth is a concrete object, so how is the word with the kasra correct for it?

I answer: the choice of this word has a fine and striking effect in describing the earth as level and smooth, and in negating any crookedness from it in the most emphatic way. That is because if you took a piece of land, levelled it, and exerted yourself in levelling it, judged by your own eye and the eyes of those skilled in farming, and all of you agreed that no crookedness remained in it at all, then you consulted an engineer about it and asked him to test its evenness against geometric measures, he would find crookedness in it in more than one place. This cannot be perceived by the sense of sight but only by geometric measurement. Thus God, Mighty and Exalted, negated that crookedness which is so fine and subtle as to escape perception, except by the measurement known to the person of calculation and geometry. Since that crookedness is perceived only by measurement and not by the senses, it was assimilated to abstract meanings, and so it was described as ʿiwaj with a kasra.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 108–109:

He attached "the Day" (al-yawm) to the time of the mountains being blown away in His saying ﴿On that day﴾, meaning: the day when they are blown away. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) after a substitute of "the Day of Resurrection." The intended meaning is the caller to the gathering (al-hashr). They said: he is Israfil, standing upon the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, calling the people, and they will come from every direction toward his direction, without deviating, ﴿with no crookedness in it﴾, meaning: no one being called will deviate from him; rather they will proceed straight toward him, without turning aside, following his voice. That is: the voices will be lowered from the intensity of terror and will be hushed (wa-khaffat) [[His saying "wa-khaffat" — in al-Sihah, "khafata al-sawt" means it became quiet. (Ea)]], ﴿so you will hear nothing but whispering (hamsan)﴾, which is the hidden sound. From it come the whispered letters (al-huruf al-mahmusa). It was said: it derives from the whispering of camels (hams al-ibil), which is the sound of their hooves when they walk, meaning: you will hear nothing but the padding of feet and their movement toward the gathering. Who is fit to be in the nominative and the accusative: the nominative is in apposition (badal) to "the intercession," with an ellipsed genitive (muda𝑓) implied, meaning: intercession will not benefit except the intercession of the one whom ﴿the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. The accusative is as object (maf'ul). The meaning of "permitted for him" and ﴿was pleased with for him﴾ is "for his sake": that is, He permitted the intercessor and was pleased with his speech for his sake. Similar to this lam is the lam in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾.

(Ea)]], ﴿so you will hear nothing but whispering (hamsan)﴾, which is the hidden sound. From it come the whispered letters (al-huruf al-mahmusa). Similar to this lam is the lam in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾.
He knows what is before them of circumstances and what they are yet to face, while they do not encompass His knowledge with their own knowledge.

The phrase "al-wujuh" (faces) here refers to the faces of the disobedient sinners. When they witness on the Day of Resurrection the disappointment, the misery and the evil of the reckoning, their faces become ʿaniya (cast down, humbled and submissive), like the faces of the ʿanat (captives, prisoners). A similar expression is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When they see it [the punishment] approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾, and ﴿Faces that Day will be gloomy﴾. As for His, the Exalted, saying ﴿And he has failed who carries [the burden of] injustice﴾, and what follows it, it is a parenthetical statement (iʿtiraḍ), like your saying: "They have failed and lost." And everyone who commits injustice is a failure and a loser.

Injustice (al-zulm) is that one takes from his companion beyond his right. Diminution (al-hadm) is that one cuts short the right of his brother and does not give it to him in full, like the description of the defrauders (al-Mutaffifin), who, when they take measure from people, take in full, and when they measure or weigh for them, they cause loss. That is: he will not fear the recompense of injustice or diminution, because he has neither done injustice nor diminished. It is also recited as ﴿فلا يخف﴾ (so let him not fear), in the prohibitive form.

And thus (وَكَذلِكَ) is coordinated with "thus" (كَذلِكَ نَقُصُّ), i.e., "like that" [the sending down]: just as We sent down these verses containing the warning, [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is: just as We sent down these verses containing the warning... etc." Ahmad said: The correct interpretation of it is:

"so that they may be in hope of taqwa (God-consciousness) and remembrance; otherwise, if God had willed taqwa from all of them, it would have occurred. Similar expressions have already passed. And it is astonishing that he (al-Zamakhshari) quoted from Sibawayh, in explaining la'alla (perhaps) at the beginning of this surah, at the words of the Exalted, "perhaps he will remember or fear" (لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشى), that its meaning is: "be upon your hope," then he retracted this here, because the corrupt belief drives him to this false interpretation. And God is the Granter of success.]] We sent down the whole Qur'an in this manner, repeating in it the verses of warning, so that they would be in a state where abandoning sins or doing good and obedience is desired from them. And remembrance (al-dhikr), as we have mentioned, applies to obedience and worship. It was also read as nuhdith and tuhdith, with the letters nun and ta, meaning: you (tuhdith) cause to occur. Some of them pronounced the thaʼ with a sukun for lightness, as in:

فاليوم أشرب غير مستحقب ... إثما من الله ولا واغل
[[حلت لي الخمر وكنت امرأ ... عن شربها في شغل شاغل

فاليوم أشرب غير مستحقب ... إثما من الله ولا واغل

For Imru' al-Qays, who had sworn not to drink wine until he killed the Banu Asad who had killed his father Hujr. When he had killed a group of them he said:

Wine has become lawful for me after it was forbidden to me, and I was preoccupied, with a preoccupation that kept me from drinking it. Today I drink, having taken vengeance, and it should have been in the nominative (fa-al-yawma ashrabu) because there was no jussive particle, but it was given sukun for the sake of the meter. The mustahqib of a thing is one who carries it on his back, from which comes "haqiba" (saddlebag), so sin is likened to a thing carried, due to its burden upon the soul; istihqab here is imaginative. The wa'il is one who enters upon drinkers without being invited; i.e., "today I drink whatever I wish, not bearing any sin from God, since I have fulfilled my oath, nor as an uninvited intruder upon the drinkers."]]

Then exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth. This is an expression of magnification of Him and of what He directs His servants with, through His commands and prohibitions, His promise and His threat, and the disposition between His reward and His punishment according to their deeds, and other things that the affair of His dominion carries out. When He had mentioned the Qur'an and its sending down, He said, by way of digression (istitrad): ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed; and say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾ — no, the text reads: "And when Jibril recites to you what is revealed to you of the Qur'an, then wait patiently until he has finished reciting it to you, and then recite it after that, and do not let your recitation run ahead of his." A similar statement is His, exalted is He: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾.

It has also been said that its meaning is: do not convey what was ambiguous (mujmal) from it until the clarification comes to you. And it was read: "until its revelation is concluded to you" (hatta tuqda ilayka wahyuhu).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ includes humility before Allah and thankfulness to Him for what is known of the order of learning, meaning: "You have taught me, O Lord, a subtle point regarding the field of learning and a beautiful manner which I did not have before, so increase me in knowledge upon knowledge, for You have wisdom and knowledge in everything."

It has also been said: Allah did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 115:

It is said in the commands of kings and their injunctions: "The king addressed (taqaddama) so-and-so, instructed him (awza'a ilayhi), resolved upon him (azama 'alayhi), and charged him (ʿahida ilayhi)." God, glory be to Him, linked the story of Adam to His words ﴿And We have diversified in it [this Qur'an] some of the warning, that they might fear God﴾, and the meaning is:

And He swore an oath: "Indeed We commanded their father Adam and enjoined upon him that he not approach this tree, and threatened him with being included among the wrongdoers if he approached it. That was before their existence and before We threatened them. Yet he turned aside to what he had been forbidden, and when he committed it he disregarded the threat, just as they disregard it." It is as if He is saying: the foundation of the affair of the children of Adam rests on this, and their roots are firmly set in it.

If you ask: what is meant by "forgetting" (al-nisyan)? I answer: it may be taken to mean forgetting, which is the opposite of remembering, meaning that he did not give the commandment the sincere attention it deserved, nor did he secure it by fixing it in his heart and binding his soul to it, so that forgetting arose from that. It may also be taken to mean abandonment, meaning that he abandoned what he had been enjoined regarding guarding against the tree and eating its fruit.

It is also read as ﴿fa-nasiya﴾, that is, the Satan caused him to forget.

Resolve (al-'azm): determination and persistence in abstaining from eating, and that he should be firm in this with a firmness that would dispel Satan's hope of enticing him.

Wujud (finding/existence): It may be in the sense of knowledge ('ilm), with its two objects being ﴿'azman﴾ (resolve). Or it may be the opposite of non-existence (ʿadam), as if he said: "and We did not find in him resolve" (wa-ʿadamna lahu ʿazman).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 116:

"Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And remember the time when there befell him (Adam) the enmity of Iblis, his whispering to him, and his adorning for him the eating from the tree, and his obedience to him, after advice and an eloquent admonition and a warning against his scheming had preceded with him, so that it becomes clear to you that he was not among the people of firm resolve and steadfastness."

If you say: Iblis was a jinn, as is shown by the words of the Exalted, ﴿He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [18:50]. Then how did the command reach him when it was specific to the angels? I say: He was in their company, and he worshipped God the Exalted in their manner of worship. So when they were commanded to prostrate to Adam and to humble themselves before him as an honour to him, the jinn who was with them was more worthy to humble himself, just as, if a person enters an assembly and the nobles and chiefs of its people stand up for him, the one among them who is lower in rank is more obliged to stand, and if he does not stand, he is blamed. It was said to him: "So-and-so and so-and-so have stood; who are you that you should disdain to stand?"

If you say: How then is his exception valid when he was a jinn and not one of the angels? I say: The rule of predominance (taghlib) was applied in using the name "angels" for them and for him, so the exception was made on that basis, like your saying: "They went out except so-and-so," referring to a woman among men.

"Aba" (refused) is a new independent sentence, as if it were the answer to someone who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The preferred view is that no object should be supposed for it, namely the prostration indicated by His words ﴿so they prostrated﴾, and that its meaning is: he showed refusal, hesitation and reluctance.

Then let him not drive you both out of the Garden, so that you would be left in misery (fa-la yukhrijannakuma: "let him not be the cause of your expulsion").

As for the attribution of misery (al-shaqa') to Adam alone, and not to Hawwa', although both were included in the expulsion: this is because the misery of the man, who is the guardian (qayyim) and leader (amir) of his household, contains within it their misery, just as his happiness contains their happiness. So the speech is abbreviated by attributing it to him alone, while the rhyme (al-fasila) is maintained.

Or the "misery" is meant as the toil of seeking sustenance, and that is tied to the head of the household, the man, and it returns to him. It is related that a red ox was sent down to Adam, and he would plough with it and wipe the sweat from his brow.

It has been read as wa-annaka with a kasra and with a fatha. The reasoning for the fatha is that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon an-la taju' (that you will not hunger). If you say: "La enters upon an (that), so one does not say: inna an Zaydan munṭaliq" — and the waw stands in for inna and takes its place, so why has it entered upon it? I say: the waw was not set to be always a substitute for inna; rather it substitutes for every governing particle (kull 'amil). Since it is not a particle set specifically for emphasis (tahqiq) like inna, their combination is not prohibited, as the combination of inna and an is prohibited.

The satiety, the quenching of thirst, the clothing, and the shelter: these are the pillars on which a person's sustenance turns. [[Mahmud said: "He mentioned the categories by which human existence is sustained, etc." Ahmad said: This is a fine observation. The verse contains a wonderful rhetorical secret called *qat' al-nazir 'an al-nazir* (cutting a thing off from its counterpart), in that it separates thirst from hunger and sun-exposure from clothing, despite the correspondence between them. The purpose of this is to establish the enumeration of these blessings and to classify them. Had each been paired with its own kind, the enumerated items might be mistaken for a single blessing. Scholars of rhetoric have long and recently noticed the subtlety of this meaning, and the first al-Kindi said:

As if I had never ridden a horse for pleasure,
nor embraced a maiden wearing anklets,
and had never sipped cool wine,
nor said to my horses, "Return, a charge after a rout!"

Here he separated riding a horse from his saying "Return, a charge after a rout," and separated embracing a maiden from sipping the cup, while keeping the correspondence. His aim was to enumerate and multiply his pleasures and boasts. The second al-Kindi followed him and said:

You stood, and no standing man doubted death,
as if you were in the sheath of destruction while it slept.
Heroes pass by you in full flight,
while your face is bright and your smile is wide.

Sayf al-Dawla objected to him that this does not contain the cutting of a thing from its counterpart. But despite his acumen, his understanding fell short of what the hand of Abu al-Tayyib reached in this great and wonderful meaning. Moreover, this verse contains an additional secret beyond what was mentioned, namely the intention to match the *fawasil* (verse-endings). Had thirst been joined with hunger, saying "Indeed, for you therein is that you will not hunger or thirst," the string of verse-endings would have been scattered, whereas now it is arranged in order. And God knows best.]] So He mentioned their collective provision for him in Paradise, and that he is sufficiently provided for, needing neither a provider's sustenance nor a earner's effort, as the people of this world need. He mentioned them in negative form, by their opposites, which are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and sun-exposure [[His words "al-dahw" (sun-exposure): in al-Sihah, it is said: "I exposed myself to the sun (*dahaytu lil-shams*) — *dahan* (with a long vowel) — when the sun came out for me, and *dahaytu* (with a fatha) is similar." (Ayn)]], so that the hearing of the one addressed would be struck by the names of the categories of misery against which he has been warned, so that he would avoid the cause that leads to them out of aversion to them.

The satiety, the quenching of thirst, the clothing, and the shelter: these are the pillars on which a person's sustenance turns. [[Mahmud said: "He mentioned the categories by which human existence is sustained, etc." Ahmad said: This is a fine observation. The verse contains a wonderful rhetorical secret called *qat' al-nazir 'an al-nazir* (cutting a thing off from its counterpart), in that it separates thirst from hunger and sun-exposure from clothing, despite the correspondence between them. The purpose of this is to establish the enumeration of these blessings and to classify them. Had each been paired with its own kind, the enumerated items might be mistaken for a single blessing. Scholars of rhetoric have long and recently noticed the subtlety of this meaning, and the first al-Kindi said:

As if I had never ridden a horse for pleasure,
nor embraced a maiden wearing anklets,
and had never sipped cool wine,
nor said to my horses, "Return, a charge after a rout!"

Here he separated riding a horse from his saying "Return, a charge after a rout," and separated embracing a maiden from sipping the cup, while keeping the correspondence. His aim was to enumerate and multiply his pleasures and boasts. The second al-Kindi followed him and said:

You stood, and no standing man doubted death,
as if you were in the sheath of destruction while it slept.
Heroes pass by you in full flight,
while your face is bright and your smile is wide.

Sayf al-Dawla objected to him that this does not contain the cutting of a thing from its counterpart. But despite his acumen, his understanding fell short of what the hand of Abu al-Tayyib reached in this great and wonderful meaning. Moreover, this verse contains an additional secret beyond what was mentioned, namely the intention to match the *fawasil* (verse-endings). Had thirst been joined with hunger, saying "Indeed, for you therein is that you will not hunger or thirst," the string of verse-endings would have been scattered, whereas now it is arranged in order. And God knows best.]] So He mentioned their collective provision for him in Paradise, and that he is sufficiently provided for, needing neither a provider's sustenance nor a earner's effort, as the people of this world need. He mentioned them in negative form, by their opposites, which are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and sun-exposure [[His words "al-dahw" (sun-exposure): in al-Sihah, it is said: "I exposed myself to the sun (*dahaytu lil-shams*) — *dahan* (with a long vowel) — when the sun came out for me, and *dahaytu* (with a fatha) is similar." (Ayn)]], so that the hearing of the one addressed would be struck by the names of the categories of misery against which he has been warned, so that he would avoid the cause that leads to them out of aversion to them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 120:

If you say: how does (waswasa) (to whisper) govern (ʿaddā) sometimes with the preposition (lām) in His words ﴿So Satan whispered to them both﴾ and at other times with (ilā)?

I say: The whispering of Satan is like the wailing of the bereaved woman (kawlawat al-thakla) [[His words "kawlawat al-thakla" mean the grieving woman. (ʿA)]], the howling of the wolf (waʿwaʿat al-dhi’b), and the clucking of the hen (waqawqat al-dajāja), in that they are imitations of sounds, and their judgment is the judgment of a sound and a noise. From this comes: "waswasa al-mubarsam" (the one with delirium whispered), and he is "mawsūs" with a kasra.

The fatha is a grammatical error (laḥn). Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited:

*Waswasa yadʿū mukhliṣan rabba al-falaq*
*sirran wa-qad aawwana taʾwīna al-ʿaqaq*
*fī al-zarab law yamḍagh sharban mā baṣaq*

These are by Ruʾba, describing a hunter (qānis). *Waswasa* means he spoke to himself; *yadʿū mukhliṣan* means he calls upon God, sincerely, that He make him capture the game. His words *sirran* he placed in the position of an adverb for emphasis, i.e., it is attached to *waswasa*; and for establishing a new meaning if it is attached to *yadʿū*, in which case the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya) explaining the whispering. *Qad aawwana* means: the wild asses (al-ḥumur al-waḥshiyya) have become (pregnant); this clause is also circumstantial. *Taʾwīn* is the filling of both flanks with the *aun*, which is the side of a full saddlebag (al-khurj al-mumtali’). *Al-awthān* are the two full sides. *Al-ʿaqaq* are the pregnant ones; its singular is *ʿaqūq*, like *ʿarūs*; it is also said that it is *al-ʿaqūq*, meaning their bellies have filled with water from their great drinking, like the bellies of pregnant women in the enclosure; it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the hunter. *Al-zarab* and *al-zarba* are its screen in which he lies in ambush; and *inzarab al-qānis* means the hunter entered the zarab. His words *law yamḍagh* also have the sense of a circumstantial clause, i.e., he is still, to the extent that if he were to chew a sip (sharb), i.e., if he were to work with his mouth a quantity of his water, which is saliva, he would not spit, so that the game would not hear his sound. The original meaning of *sharb* is a share of water; he used it metaphorically for what gathers in the mouth of saliva. Between *zarab* and *sharb* there is a paronomasia (jinās) of the near kind (al-jinās al-muḍāriʿ).

So if you say: *waswasa lahu*, its meaning is "for his sake," as in his words:

*Ajris lahā yā ibna Abī Kibāsh*
*fa-mā lahā al-layla min anfāsh*
*ghayr al-surā wa-sāʾiq najjāsh*

"*Ajris*" with a cut hamza and with the unmarked sīn, i.e., a single sound for the camels in their march; so tonight they have no *infāsh*, i.e., release to pasture. *Al-surā* is night travel. *Najashat al-ibil* means I gathered the camels after dispersal. *Najjāsh* is an intensive form, i.e., they have no grazing, but only fierce travel. It is also reported as "*ujrush*" with a connected hamza and a shīn with dots, and it has the same meaning here. *Al-jars*, with the unmarked letter, is a faint sound; with the dotted letter, it is the sound of a comb in hair; and what resembles that.

The meaning of *waswasa ilayhi* is that he conveyed the whispering to him, like your saying *ḥaddatha ilayhi* (he related to him) and *asarra ilayhi* (he confided to him). He attributed the tree to *al-khuld*, which is immortality, because whoever eats from it, according to their claim, will be immortal, just as it is said of Ḥayzūm that he is "the horse of life," because whoever touches his hoofprint lives. *Wa-mulkin lā yablā* is evidence for the reading of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with them):

*illā an takūnā malakayn* (except that you become two angels), with a kasra.

*Ṭafiqa yafʿalu kadhā* (ﷲ) is like *jaʿala yafʿalu*, *akhadha*, and *anshaʾa*. Its rule for the predicate is the same as for *kāda* (to be about to): the predicate is an imperfect verb. The difference between them is a short interval: *ṭafiqa* indicates the beginning of an action, while *kāda* indicates approaching it and drawing near to it.

The reading *yakhṣifāni* (ﷲ) indicates intensity and repetition, from *khaṣafa al-naʿl*, which means to stitch the sandal with the *khaṣṣāf* (awl). The meaning is that they both attached leaves to their private parts to cover them, and these were fig leaves. It was said that the leaf was round and took this shape beneath their fingers. It was also said that their clothing was nails, and when they committed the sin it was stripped from them and these remnants were left at the tips of their fingers.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: There is no doubt that Adam did not comply with what God had prescribed for him, and he overstepped the boundary of obedience, and that is disobedience. When he disobeyed, his act was taken out of the category of right guidance and good, so it was necessarily *ghayy* (error), because *ghayy* is the opposite of *rushd* (right guidance). But God's words ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ use this absolute expression and this explicit statement, and He did not say: "Adam slipped, erred, and so forth," which are expressions used for slips and lapses. In this there is kindness to the responsible servants, a powerful deterrent, and a comprehensive admonition. It is as if it were said to them: Look and take heed how the infallible Prophet, the beloved of God, who is not permitted to commit anything except a minor sin that does not repel, was censured for his slip with this mistake and this harsh wording. So do not be lax about the evil deeds and minor sins that you commit, let alone dare to fall into major sins.

And from some of them: ﴿fa-ghawā﴾ (so he erred) read as *fa-bashima* (so he suffered from indigestion) from excessive eating. This, even if it is valid according to the dialect of those who turn a *yā'* preceded by a *kasra* into an *alif*, so that they say *fanā* and *baqā* for *fanī* and *baqiya*, and they are the Banū Ṭayyiʾ, is a corrupt interpretation.

Question: what is the meaning of "then his Lord chose him" (thumma ijtabahu rabbuhu)? Answer: Then He accepted him after his repentance and brought him near to Himself, from "jaba ila kadhā" (he gathered to me such-and-such), so "ijtabaytuhu" (I gathered it to me). Its parallel is: "jallaytu 'alayya al-'arūsa fa-ijtalaytuhā" (the bride was unveiled to me, so I beheld her). And from the same root is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not chosen one?"﴾ (lawlā ijtabaytahā), meaning: "Why did you not gather it to yourself and choose it?" The root of the word is gathering. They say: "ijtabat al-faras nafsahā" (the mare gathered herself), when she gathers herself back together after bolting. "Wa-hadā" means He guided him, that is, He granted him success in preserving repentance and in other means of protection and piety.

Since Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them) were the first of mankind and the two sources from which humanity came into being and branched out, they were treated as if they were the whole of mankind in themselves, so they were addressed in the manner of addressing many, and so it was said: ﴿Then, if there comes to you﴾ in the plural form.

Its parallel is the attribution of an action to its cause, when in reality it belongs to what it causes: ﴿guidance﴾, meaning the Book and the Law. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that God guaranteed to whoever follows the Qur'an that he will not go astray in this world and will not be wretched in the Hereafter, then he recited His saying: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, he will not go astray, nor will he be distressed﴾. The meaning is that wretchedness in the Hereafter is the punishment of one who strayed in this world from the path of the religion. So whoever follows the Book of God, complies with its commands and refrains from its prohibitions, is saved from straying and from its punishment.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 20, verses 124–126:

Al-ḍank (a noun that applies equally to the masculine and the feminine when used as a description). It has also been read ḍankan on the pattern fa'lā. The meaning is this: with religion comes submission (al-taslīm), contentment (al-qanā'a), and reliance upon God and upon His apportionment. Its possessor spends what he has been provided with ease and generosity, and so he lives a spacious life, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Surely We shall give him a good life﴾. As for one who turns away from religion, he is dominated by greed, which never ceases to drive him toward seeking more of this world, and he is afflicted by stinginess, which holds his hand back from spending. So his life is constricted (ḍank) and his state is dark, as some of the Sufis said: "No one turns away from the remembrance of his Lord except that his time becomes dark for him and his provision becomes disturbed for him." Among the disbelievers are those upon whom God has imposed humiliation and destitution because of their disbelief. God the Exalted said: ﴿And humiliation and destitution were stamped upon them, and they incurred wrath from God. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾. He also said: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾. And He said: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been conscious of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾. And He said: ﴿Ask forgiveness of your Lord; indeed He is ever Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾. And He said: ﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾.

From al-Hasan: it is al-ḍarī' (a thorny plant of the Hellfire) and al-zaqqūm (a tree) in the Fire. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the punishment of the grave.

It has been read ﴿wa-nahshuruhu﴾ with a jazm (apocopation), in coordination with the position (maḥall) of ﴿fa-inna lahu ma'īshatan ḍankan﴾, because it is the response of the conditional. It has also been read ﴿wa-nahshuruhu﴾ with a sukūn on the hā', following the pronunciation of pause (lafẓ al-waqf). This is like His saying: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾. And just as al-zurq (the blue-eyed, i.e., the blind) was explained as blindness, so too: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., "like that you did," then He explained that: "Our signs came to you clear and luminous, but you did not look at them with the eye of one who takes heed, nor did you perceive, and you left them and became blind to them. Likewise today We leave you upon your blindness and do not remove its covering from your eyes."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 127:

When He threatened the one who turns away from His remembrance with two punishments, a constricted life in this world and being raised up blind on the Day of Resurrection, He concluded the verses of warning with His saying, ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾. It is as if He said: the raising up in blindness, which never ceases, is more severe than the narrowness of a life that comes to an end. Or he meant: our leaving him in blindness is more severe and more lasting than his leaving Our signs.

The subject (fāʿil, grammatical subject) of فَلَمْ يَهْدِ is the clause that follows it, meaning: "Did it not make clear to them" this matter, in its sense and content. A parallel is His saying ﴿And We left for him among the later generations: Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾, meaning: We left upon him this statement. It is also permissible that the implied subject be a pronoun referring to God or to the Messenger, and the reading with the first-person plural nūn supports this. Another reading is يَمْشُونَ (yamshūna, "they walk"), meaning that Quraysh travel about in the lands of ʿĀd and Thamūd and walk through their dwellings, witnessing the traces of their destruction.

The preceding word: it is the promise of deferring their recompense until the Hereafter. He says: were it not for this promise, the like of Our destroying 'Ad and Thamud would necessarily have been binding upon these disbelievers. Al-lizam (what is binding) is either a verbal noun (masdar) of lazima, described by it, or it is fi'al in the sense of mif'al, meaning mulzam (that which binds), as if it were the very instrument of binding, because of its intense bindingness, just as they say: lazaz khasm (a most stubborn adversary). And "a term appointed" (ajal musamma) cannot be free of being either conjoined to "kalima" (word) or to the pronoun in "lakana" (it would have been), meaning: the immediate punishment and an appointed term would have been binding upon them, just as both were binding upon 'Ad and Thamud. The appointed term does not stand alone apart from the immediate punishment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 130:

﴿Glorify the praises of your Lord﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while you are praising your Lord for having guided you to glorify Him and having helped you to do so. By glorification (tasbīh) is meant prayer (ṣalāt). Or it may be taken literally: he placed the verb before the times at the beginning and the times before the verb at the end, as if he had said: "Pray to God before the rising of the sun," meaning the dawn prayer, "and before its setting," meaning the noon and afternoon prayers, because these two fall in the latter half of the day, between the decline of the sun and its setting. "And glorify Him in the hours of the night and the extremities of the day," devoting these times specifically to your prayer. This is because the best remembrance is that which is done at night, for it gathers the heart, calms the body, and secludes one with the Lord. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech﴾ [73:6], and He said: ﴿Is one who worships devoutly during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾ [39:9]. Moreover, since the night is the time of tranquility and rest, when one turns it to worship it is harder and more burdensome upon the soul and more exhausting for the body, so it is closer to the meaning of obligation and more excellent in God's sight. The glorification in the hours of the night includes the ʿatamah prayer (the night prayer), and in the extremities of the day the maghrib (sunset) prayer and the dawn prayer, by way of repetition, intending specificity, just as the prayer was singled out in His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [2:238], according to some exegetes.

If you say: what is the reason for His saying "the extremities of the day" in the plural, when there are only two extremities, as He said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [11:114]? I say: the reason is to avoid ambiguity, and the dual form would add clarity. A parallel to the occurrence of the two forms in the two verses is their occurrence in the verse:

Their two backs are like the backs of two shields,
Two deserts, sandy and rugged, two times...
Their two backs are like the backs of two shields

I crossed them with one description, not with two descriptions.

This is by Khatam al-Mujashi'i. It is also said to be by Hamyan ibn Qahafa. The mahmah is the desolate wasteland. The qadhf (with a fatḥah on the qāf and sukūn on the dhāl) is that which throws its traveler out, so no one remains in it; it is also said to mean "distant." The marit (with sukūn) is the barren land with neither water nor vegetation. The turs is an animal with a protruding back. The dual "their two backs" (ẓahrāhumā) is in its original form, and it was made plural afterward to avoid ambiguity, and because the combination of two duals is sometimes disliked, especially when duals follow one another as here. The grammarians (al-nuḥāt) said: every dual that is semantically a construct is governed by what it contains, and in its wording the plural is preferred because of the multiplicity of its meaning and the dislike of combining two duals in the wording. It is permissible to keep it in its original form, as here, and it is permissible to use the singular, as in the line:

O dove of the valley's two sides, sing on.

The "jawāb" here is the cut (qaṭʿ, i.e., the disjunction). The "nuʿt" is the description. The variant reading "bi-l-simt" ("by the bearing") is also reported, and the simt means the appearance, the intention, the direction, and the path. The meaning is that they were described, or that their form was mentioned to him only once. He says: "How many two barren deserts there are with no companion in them, with two raised backs like the backs of two shields, which I crossed by travelling with one description, not by their being described to me twice or three times like others." It is also permissible that the meaning is "by mentioning one of their attributes, not by mentioning two attributes," so the nuʿt means the attribute that subsists in the thing. The passage indicates his bravery and skill.

It is also read: "and the extremities of the day," in coordination with "the hours of the night." Perhaps "la-ʿalla" ("perhaps") is for the addressee, meaning: remember God at these times, hoping and expecting that you may attain from God that by which your soul is pleased and your heart is gladdened. It is also read "tarḍā" ("you may be pleased"), meaning that your Lord will please you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 131:

﴿And do not strain your eyes﴾: that is, the gaze of your eyes. Extending the gaze means prolonging it, not letting it return, out of admiration for the thing looked upon, approval of it, and wishing that it were one's own, as the onlookers of Qarun did when they said, ﴿Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is a person of great fortune.﴾ until those who were given knowledge and faith said to them, ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds.﴾ In this there is the implication that a gaze that is not prolonged is pardoned, like the gaze of one who glances at a thing and then lowers his eyes. Since looking at adornments is, as it were, fixed in human nature, and whoever sees something of them loves to extend his gaze toward it and fill his eyes with it, it was said: ﴿And do not strain your eyes﴾, that is, do not do what you are accustomed to and habituated to. The scholars of piety have stressed the obligation to lower the gaze from the buildings of the wrongdoers and the finery of the wicked in clothing, mounts and other things, because they only make these things for the eyes of onlookers; so the one who looks at them fulfils their purpose, and is, as it were, an incitement to them to make such things. ﴿Pairs of them﴾: categories of disbelievers. It is permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun ha' (the suffix), with the verb governing ﴿minhum﴾ (of them), as if he said: toward that with which We have provided enjoyment, namely categories of them and some people from among them. If you say: On what is ﴿zahrata﴾ (the splendour) put in the accusative? I say: On one of four aspects: on blame, which is the accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ); on the reading in which mata'na (We have provided enjoyment) is taken to mean a'ṭainā (We gave) and khawwalna (We bestowed), with it being a second object; on its being a substitute (badal) for the place of the prepositional phrase; and on its being a substitute for ﴿azwājan﴾, with the implied meaning "possessors of splendour."

If you say: What is the meaning of ﴿zahra﴾ according to the one who vocalised the ha' with a fatḥa? I say: the meaning of zahra is itself, namely adornment and radiance, as in the saying "al-jahra" in "jahratan" (openly). And it has been read: "Show us Allah openly (jahratan)." It may also be the plural of zāhir (bright), as a description of them, meaning that they are the bright ones of this world, because of the clearness of their colours from what they amuse themselves with and enjoy, the brightness of their faces, the splendour of their appearance and their insignia, in contrast to what the believers and the righteous have of pallor of complexion and austerity in garments, ﴿so that We may test them﴾: that We may try them, so that they deserve punishment, because of the ingratitude found in them. Or that We may punish them in the Hereafter because of it. ﴿And the provision of your Lord﴾: it is what He has stored up for him of the reward of the Hereafter, which is better in itself and more lasting. Or what He has provided him of the blessing of Islam and prophethood. Or because their wealth is predominantly from usurpation, theft and what is forbidden, in some respects. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is that the sustenance of these who enjoy themselves in this world is mostly acquired from the unlawful ..." etc. Ahmad said: Were it not that the aim of the Qadariyya in this is to establish a provider other than Allah, just as they established a creator other than Allah, the discussion would be merely verbal. The truth and the Sunna is that everything by which a creature is sustained is a provision from Allah, whether lawful or otherwise; it does not follow from Allah's being the one who provides it that it must be lawful. Just as Allah creates through the hand of the servant what He has forbidden him, so He provides him what He has permitted him to consume and what ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. And Allah is the one who grants success and correctness.] And the lawful is ﴿better and more lasting﴾, because Allah does not attribute to Himself except what is lawful and good, not what is forbidden and foul, and the forbidden is not called provision at all. [His saying "the forbidden is not called provision at all" is the view of the Mu'tazila; according to the people of the Sunna it is called provision.]

It is related from Abdullah ibn Qasit, from Rafi', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me to a Jew and said: "Say to him: The Messenger of Allah says to you, lend me [something] until Rajab." He said: "By Allah, I will not lend it except against a pledge." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I am trustworthy in heaven and I am trustworthy on earth; carry to him my iron coat of mail." So it was revealed: ﴿And do not strain your eyes﴾.

[I say: There is a distortion in the narrators here. It is actually from Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qasit, from Abu Rafi'; perhaps this is an error of the copyists. The hadith is recorded by Ishaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, al-Tabari and al-Tabarani through this route in extended form. In its chain is Musa ibn Ubayda al-Zubayri, who is abandoned (matruk). It is cited as evidence against the validity of what he narrated that it contains that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward that with which We have provided enjoyment to pairs of them﴾ and the verse, was revealed concerning this incident, whereas Surah Ta-Ha is Meccan, and this incident occurred in Medina, as in the Sahih. This can be answered, since there is no barrier to the verse alone being Medinan while the rest of the surah is Meccan. As for interpreting it as multiple occurrences of the incident, that is not correct.]

And command your family to prayer, and be steadfast in it yourself. That is: turn, you and your family, to the worship of God and to prayer, and seek help through it in your need. Do not concern yourself with the matter of provision and livelihood, for your provision is secured by Us: We are the ones who provide for you, and We do not ask you to provide for yourself or your family. So free your mind for the matter of the Hereafter.

Something similar in meaning is the saying of people: "Whoever submits (dāna, from dān: to be humbled, and dānahu: to humble him, as in al-Sihah) in the work of God, God will be in his work." (ʿ)

It is related from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr that whenever he saw what the rulers possessed, he would recite ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them...﴾ and then call out: "Prayer, prayer, may God have mercy on you."

It is related from Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani that whenever his family was afflicted by poverty, he would say: "Stand and pray. With this God commanded His Messenger," and then he would recite this verse.

They proposed, in keeping with their habit of obstinacy, a sign as proof of prophethood. So it was said to them: "Has there not come to them a sign that is the mother of signs and the greatest of them in the matter of inimitability," meaning the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is the proof of what is in the other revealed books and the evidence of their soundness, since it is a miracle, whereas those (other books) are not miracles. Thus they are in need of its testimony to the soundness of what is in them, the need of one who is argued against for the testimony of the proof. It is also read as ﴿الصُّحُفِ﴾ with the lightened (ta') form. The pronoun referring back to "the clear proof" (al-bayyinah) is masculine because it carries the meaning of proof (burhan) and evidence (dalil).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 20, verse 135:

Each of us, meaning each one of us and of you, is *mutarabbis* (waiting) for the outcome and for what our affair and your affair will come to.

It is also read as *al-sawa'* (السواء), meaning the middle and the good. Or *al-mustawi* (المستوى), *al-su'* (السوء), *al-su'a* (السوأى), and *al-sawiyy* (السوي), which is the diminutive of *al-su'* (السوء).

It is also read as *fa-tamatta'u fa-sawfa ta'lamun* (فتمتعوا فسوف تعلمون). Abu Rafi' said: "I memorized it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Ta-Ha, he will be given on the Day of Resurrection the reward of the Muhajirun and the Ansar." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi through the transmission of Ziyad from al-Hasan, as a *mursal* report.] He also said: "The people of Paradise will recite from the Qur'an only Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin." [Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
